a: After Joshua died
t: A book that opens with a death
p: Judges begins as Joshua began, with the death of a leader. But this time no successor is named.
b: Joshua opens "After the death of Moses the servant of the LORD" (Joshua 1:1), and the LORD at once names Joshua as the new leader. Judges opens the same way, but no one takes Joshua's place. Israel must ask God who will lead, and the answer is a tribe, not a person. The book then tells of Joshua's death a second time (2:6–9), almost word for word from Joshua 24:28–31. Most scholars think Judges has two introductions: 1:1–2:5 looks at the land not taken, tribe by tribe, and 2:6–3:6 sets out the moral pattern the rest of the book follows. The first may look back on events after Joshua; the second steps back to his lifetime.

a: asked the LORD
p: "Asked the LORD" means asking for an answer from God, probably by the priest's sacred lots.
b: The Hebrew sha'al be-YHWH, "ask by the LORD," is the regular phrase for seeking a yes-or-no or this-or-that answer from God, usually through the high priest and the Urim and Thummim (Numbers 27:21; 1 Samuel 14:37; 1 Samuel 23:2–4). The same question, "Who will go up first for us?", and the same answer, "Judah," come back at the end of the book, when Israel goes to war against its own tribe of Benjamin (20:18). The book is framed by two holy wars: the first against the Canaanites, the last against an Israelite tribe. That frame already hints at the book's slide.

a: the LORD
p: "The LORD" in small capitals stands for God's personal name, YHWH. See the book introduction.
b: Where the Hebrew has God's name, the four letters YHWH, the Plain English writes "the LORD," following the old Jewish practice of saying Adonai, "my Lord," instead of the name. "God" translates Elohim, a general word. The book introduction explains the convention.

a: Judah is the one to go up
p: Judah leads the attack, and its story gets the most space. Many readers see a quiet case for Judah's later kings.
b: In Joshua the attack on Canaan was led by all Israel under one man. Here the tribes act one at a time, and Judah goes first. Judah's campaign gets fifteen verses and is a list of successes (1:2–20); the northern tribes get a list of failures (1:21–36). Many scholars, such as Marc Brettler and Barry Webb, read the chapter as written from Judah's point of view, preparing for David, a man of Judah, and contrasting him with Saul of Benjamin, whose tribe fails first (1:21). Traditional readers note that Jacob's blessing had already given Judah the lead (Genesis 49:8–10). Othniel, the first judge, is also from Judah (3:9).

a: the land that fell to me by lot
p: Simeon's towns lay inside Judah's land in the far south, so the two tribes fought together.
b: The Hebrew says "my lot" and "your lot," the land each tribe received when lots were cast before the LORD (Joshua 14:2; Joshua 18:10). Simeon's share was a set of towns in the Negev inside Judah's borders (Joshua 19:1–9). Jacob had said that Simeon would be scattered in Israel (Genesis 49:7), and in later times Simeon seems to have been absorbed into Judah. Simeon is missing from Moses' blessing in Deuteronomy 33 and from the Song of Deborah (Judges 5). The two tribes were "brothers," sons of Leah, so the alliance also reads as family loyalty.

a: ten thousand men
p: The Hebrew word for "thousand" can also mean a clan or a fighting unit, which may make some numbers smaller.
b: Judges has many large round numbers: ten thousand at Bezek, ten thousand Moabites (3:29), a hundred and twenty thousand Midianites (8:10), forty-two thousand Ephraimites (12:6). The Hebrew 'elef means "thousand," but it also means a clan or the troop a clan sent to war (6:15, where Gideon's "clan" is an 'elef). Some scholars, following George Mendenhall, read many of these figures as counts of units: "ten units" rather than ten thousand men. Others take the numbers as given or as round figures meant to show size. The question is the same one raised by the censuses in Numbers.

a: Adoni-bezek
p: Adoni-bezek means "lord of Bezek," a title more than a name. He may be the same as Adoni-zedek of Jerusalem.
b: Bezek is usually placed at Khirbet Ibziq, northeast of Shechem (1 Samuel 11:8), though a southern site near Jerusalem has been suggested because Judah fights here. Adoni-bezek is taken to Jerusalem after his defeat (1:7), and he sounds much like Adoni-zedek, the king of Jerusalem who led five kings against Joshua (Joshua 10:1–3). In Joshua 10 the Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus, in fact calls that king Adonibezek. Many scholars think the two traditions are related; others think they are two different men with similar titles.

a: they cut off the thumbs of his hands and the big toes of his feet
p: A man without thumbs cannot hold a sword or bow, and without big toes he cannot run or stand firm in battle.
b: Cutting off thumbs and big toes left a warrior unable to fight while keeping him alive, and it shamed him. Greek writers record similar punishments: Athens is said to have voted to cut off the thumbs of captured rowers in the Peloponnesian War so they could row but not fight. Israel's law does not command such a thing, and the text does not say God ordered it. Adoni-bezek himself sees it as fair payback (1:7). The scene sets a theme that runs through Judges: deeds come back on the doer's own head (9:56–57).

a: What I did to others, God has now done to me.
p: A Canaanite king, not an Israelite, is the first to say that God repays deeds in kind.
b: Adoni-bezek uses the general word Elohim, "God," not the LORD's name. He accepts his fate as the measure he gave others, the principle of "eye for eye" (Exodus 21:23–25), applied by God rather than by a court. Jewish readers drew from verses like this the rabbinic rule "measure for measure" (Mishnah Sotah 1:7). Some modern readers see the brutality as Israel becoming like the Canaanites from the first chapter. Others note that the book lets an enemy speak the truth about divine justice, as it later lets a Midianite interpret a dream (7:13–14).

a: The people of Judah made war on Jerusalem and captured it.
p: Judah takes and burns Jerusalem here, yet the Jebusites still live there in 1:21 and in David's day.
b: This verse says Judah captured and burned Jerusalem. But 1:21 says Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites from it, Joshua 15:63 says Judah "could not drive out the Jebusites," and Jerusalem is still a foreign town, Jebus, in 19:10–12. David finally takes it (2 Samuel 5:6–9). Josephus explains that Judah took the lower town but not the upper fortress; other traditional readers say the Jebusites came back. Many critical scholars think two traditions stand side by side, one claiming early success for Judah and one remembering failure. Either way, the reader learns not to trust the book's victories to last.

a: They struck down Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai.
t: Who defeated the sons of Anak?
p: Joshua 15 credits Caleb, Joshua 10–11 credits Joshua, and here Judah strikes them. The three accounts overlap.
b: Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai are the "descendants of Anak" whom the spies saw at Hebron (Numbers 13:22). Joshua 15:14 says, "From there Caleb drove out the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai, descendants of Anak." Joshua 10:36–37 and 11:21 credit Joshua's army, and here the tribe of Judah strikes them, while 1:20 adds that Caleb drove them out. Traditional readers fit these together: Joshua's campaign broke Hebron, and later Caleb, leading Judah's men, cleared it for good. Critical scholars see a local Calebite tradition told in several ways. All agree that Hebron belonged to Caleb's clan.

a: Whoever attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him my daughter Achsah as his wife.
p: The story of Achsah (1:11–15) repeats Joshua 15:15–19 almost exactly.
b: The Hebrew of 1:11–15 and Joshua 15:15–19 is nearly the same, which is why the Plain English here follows the site's Joshua wording closely. Small differences: Joshua already has "Caleb's brother" (Joshua 15:17); Judges adds "younger" and names Caleb as the giver in 1:15. Kiriath-sepher means "town of the book" or "of the scribe"; its other name, Debir, may be Khirbet Rabud southwest of Hebron or Tell Beit Mirsim. Why tell it twice? Many scholars think Judges took the story from a common source to open with an ideal picture: a brave warrior, a bold daughter, a generous father, and land and water gained. It is the last time a family in Judges works like this.

a: Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother
p: The Hebrew can mean that Othniel was Caleb's younger brother, or that Kenaz was, which makes Othniel Caleb's nephew.
b: The phrase "Othniel son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb, the younger than him" can attach "brother" to Othniel or to Kenaz. Caleb's own father was Jephunneh (Numbers 13:6), so if Othniel was a brother he was a half-brother; if Kenaz was the brother, Othniel was a nephew marrying his cousin, a common match in the ancient world. The Targum and many Jewish commentators take Othniel as Caleb's brother; others prefer nephew. "Son of Kenaz" may also mean simply "a Kenizzite," the clan Caleb belonged to (Numbers 32:12), which Genesis traces to Edom (Genesis 36:11). Israel's first judge came from a family of outsiders who had joined Judah.
orig: עָתְנִיאֵל בֶּן־קְנַז אֲחִי כָלֵב הַקָּטֹן מִמֶּנּוּ (Otni'el ben-Qenaz achi Khalev haqqaton mimmennu)

a: She got down from her donkey
p: The verb for getting down is rare. It comes back once more in Judges, for Jael's tent peg going into the ground.
b: The Hebrew tsanach occurs only here, in Joshua 15:18, and in Judges 4:21, where Jael's tent peg "went down into the ground." Its meaning was already uncertain to the ancient translators. The Greek versions have Achsah "grumble" or "cry out" from her donkey, and the Vulgate has her "sigh." Most modern scholars take it as "slip down, dismount," a gesture of respect before her father, as Rebekah and Abigail get down from their mounts (Genesis 24:64; 1 Samuel 25:23). If the link to 4:21 is meant, the book opens and closes its first women's stories with the same rare word: a woman who asks and receives, and a woman who strikes.

a: Give me a blessing.
p: Achsah speaks up and gets what she asks. Many readers see her as the high point from which Judges' women decline.
b: A "blessing" here is a gift, perhaps a wedding present, and the Negev is dry land that needs water. Achsah asks boldly and her father gives more than she asked, the upper and the lower pools. Literary readers such as Cheryl Exum, Mieke Bal and Barry Webb note that the women of Judges are a measure of the book's health: Achsah is honored and provided for; Deborah and Jael lead and fight (chapters 4–5); a woman of Thebez kills a tyrant (9:53); then Jephthah's daughter is offered up, or on some readings given to lifelong service, because of her father's vow (11:34–40), Samson's women are used and betrayed (chapters 14–16), and the Levite's concubine is murdered (chapter 19). The book's first daughter is given land and water; its last daughters are taken by force (21:19–23).

a: pools of water
p: The word gullot probably means basins or springs of water, which made a dry field worth having.
b: The Hebrew gullot comes from a root meaning "round" or "roll," and seems to mean bowl-shaped pools or springs. Elsewhere it names round bowls on pillars (1 Kings 7:41) and the bowl of a lamp (Zechariah 4:2). The "upper and lower" pools may be springs at two levels of a valley. Some scholars identify them with the springs near Khirbet Rabud, a proposed site for Debir. In the dry south a field without water was nearly worthless, so Achsah's request was practical as well as bold.

a: The family of the Kenite who was Moses' father-in-law
p: The Kenites were a desert clan tied to Moses by marriage. They moved with Judah and lived on as friends of Israel.
b: Moses' father-in-law is called Jethro and Reuel, and Hobab is called his son or his father-in-law (Exodus 3:1; Exodus 2:18; Numbers 10:29; 4:11). Here he is called "the Kenite." The name Qeni is related to a word for smith, and many scholars think the Kenites were traveling metalworkers. The "City of Palms" is Jericho (Deuteronomy 34:3). The Kenites settled near Arad in the Negev, among "the people," probably Judah. Some scholars, comparing 1 Samuel 15:6, where Kenites live among the Amalekites, think the text once read "lived with the Amalekites." Later Kenites include Heber and Jael (4:11, 17) and the Rechabites (1 Chronicles 2:55; Jeremiah 35).

a: so it was named Hormah
p: Hormah sounds like cherem, the ban. The town's name means something like "Ban-town."
b: The verb "put under the ban" (hecherim) and the name Hormah (Chormah) come from the same root. Numbers 21:3 gives an earlier naming: "They devoted them and their towns to destruction, and the place was named Hormah." Traditional readers see the same town destroyed twice, or Numbers looking ahead to this event. Critical scholars see two stories explaining one name. This is the only use of the ban in Judges' conquest chapter. The next time Israel puts a town under the ban, it is the Israelite town of Jabesh-gilead (21:11).

a: But there was no driving out the people who lived in the valley, for they had iron chariots.
p: "The LORD was with Judah," yet Judah could not beat iron chariots. Readers have asked what the verse implies about God.
b: The Hebrew is short and odd: "for not to drive out." The Greek and most English versions supply "could not." Skeptics have quoted the verse to say the LORD was too weak to beat iron. Traditional readers answer that the failure was Judah's: God promised victory over chariots (Joshua 17:16–18; Deuteronomy 20:1), and the book soon shows him beating nine hundred iron chariots through Deborah and Barak (4:3, 15). On this reading the problem was Judah's faith, not God's power. Many modern scholars see the verse as plain realism: hill farmers could not fight chariot cities on the plains, which is where the archaeology shows Canaanite towns surviving into the Iron Age.

a: iron chariots
p: Probably wooden chariots with iron fittings, the tanks of the day, used in the flat valleys.
b: Chariots were light wooden vehicles drawn by two horses, carrying a driver and an archer. "Iron" probably refers to metal fittings or plating, a sign of wealth at the start of the Iron Age, around 1200 to 1000 BC, when iron was still rare. Egyptian records list hundreds of chariots captured from Canaanite city-states, for example by Thutmose III at Megiddo. Chariots needed flat ground, so they ruled the plains of Jezreel and the coast, while Israel's early villages grew in the hills where chariots were useless. Iron working itself was controlled by others for a long time (1 Samuel 13:19–22).

a: the Benjaminites did not drive them out
p: Joshua 15:63 says the same of Judah. Here it is Benjamin's failure, and Benjamin's town.
b: Joshua 15:63 reads: "But the people of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites, who lived in Jerusalem." Judges gives the same note to Benjamin and changes "could not" to "did not." Jerusalem lay on the border between the two tribes and was counted to Benjamin (Joshua 18:16, 28). The change fits the chapter's slide from Judah's success to the others' failure, and Benjamin's failure here foreshadows its near destruction at the end of the book (chapters 19–21), which begins when a Levite refuses to stay in Jebusite Jerusalem (19:10–12).

a: The town used to be called Luz.
p: Jacob named the place Bethel, "house of God," after his dream. Its Canaanite name was Luz.
b: Genesis 28:19 says Jacob "named that place Bethel, though the city was called Luz before that." Luz may mean "almond tree." The capture of Bethel here is the house of Joseph's only success in the chapter, and it is won by a spy story like the one at Jericho (Joshua 2). Bethel later became a major shrine. The ark stood there for a time (20:26–27), and Jeroboam set up a golden calf there (1 Kings 12:28–29). Archaeologists usually place it at Beitin, north of Jerusalem, where a destruction in the late Bronze Age has been reported, though the dating is debated.

a: we will treat you with loyal love
p: The spies promise hesed to a Canaanite who helps them, as at Jericho. But this man does not join Israel.
b: Loyal love (hesed) is the word of the oath to Rahab: "since I have shown you loyal love, you too will show loyal love to my father's household" (Joshua 2:12). In both stories spies find an insider, the town falls, and the helper's family is spared. But Rahab confessed Israel's God and lived among Israel (Joshua 2:11; Joshua 6:25). The man of Luz goes off to the land of the Hittites and builds a new Luz (1:26). Webb and others read the contrast as a sign of the times: Canaan is not converted, only moved. Others see no criticism here, simply an honest deal kept.

a: Manasseh did not take possession of Beth-shean and its villages or Taanach and its villages.
p: The list follows Joshua 17:11–13. These towns guarded the Jezreel Valley, the land's main east-west road.
b: Joshua 17:12 says, "But the Manassites could not take possession of these towns, because the Canaanites were set on living in that land." Beth-shean, Taanach, Ibleam, Megiddo and Dor were walled towns along the Jezreel and Beth-shean valleys and the coast. Excavations show that Beth-shean was an Egyptian garrison town into the twelfth century BC and that Megiddo stayed Canaanite into the eleventh. Israel held them only under David and Solomon (1 Kings 4:12). The tribes listed in 1:27–36 run roughly south to north, and the failures grow: first Canaanites live among Israel, then Israel lives among Canaanites (1:32–33), then Dan is pushed out altogether (1:34).

a: forced labor
p: The word mas means unpaid labor owed to a ruler. Later Israel's own kings used it on Israelites.
b: Mas is forced labor, work crews owed to a king or a stronger people. Deuteronomy allowed it only for distant towns that made peace (Deuteronomy 20:10–11), not for the peoples of the land, who were to be put under the ban (Deuteronomy 20:16–18). So Judges reports a compromise: Israel profited from the Canaanites instead of driving them out. The word comes back under Solomon, who drafted the remaining Canaanites (1 Kings 9:20–21) and then Israelites (1 Kings 5:13–14), and the anger over it split the kingdom (1 Kings 12:18).
r: Deuteronomy 20:10–18; Joshua 16:10; Joshua 17:13; 1 Kings 9:20–21; 1 Kings 5:13–14; 1 Kings 12:18

a: Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites of Gezer either
p: Gezer guarded the road from the coast to Jerusalem. It became Israelite only when Pharaoh gave it to Solomon.
b: Joshua 16:10 says, "But they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer." Gezer (Tell Jezer, west of Jerusalem) was a large walled town mentioned in Egyptian records, including the Merneptah Stele of about 1208 BC, which also names Israel. According to 1 Kings 9:16, an Egyptian king captured Gezer, burned it, and gave it as a wedding gift to his daughter, Solomon's wife. Solomon then rebuilt it. Excavators have found a six-chambered gate there that many date to the tenth century BC, though the date is debated.

a: the Asherites made their home in the middle of the Canaanites who lived in the land
p: With Asher and Naphtali the wording flips: Israel now lives among the Canaanites.
b: For Manasseh, Ephraim and Zebulun the text says the Canaanites lived among Israel. For Asher and Naphtali it says Israel lived among the Canaanites, as the minority. For Dan, the Amorites push Israel out (1:34). Literary readers such as Webb and Daniel Block see a deliberate decline across the chapter, from Judah's success to Dan's retreat. Historians see a realistic picture of how the north was settled: small groups living in the hills and valleys among the older towns of the coast and plains. Either way, the land is shared, not taken, and 2:1–5 gives God's verdict on it.

a: The Amorites crowded the Danites into the hill country.
p: Dan's failure here explains its later move north to Laish (chapter 18).
b: Dan's land lay west of Benjamin, toward the coast (Joshua 19:40–46). Squeezed by the Amorites, and later by the Philistines in Samson's day (chapters 13–16), the Danites looked for new land and took Laish in the far north, renaming it Dan (18:1–31; Joshua 19:47). Dan is also the only tribe with no Israelite leader named in this chapter, and in the Song of Deborah it "hangs around the ships" (5:17). The house of Joseph later forced these same Amorites into labor (1:35), but Dan's own story is one of retreat.

a: The border of the Amorites
p: The Scorpion Pass is far south, on Edom's border. Many scholars think the text first read "Edomites."
b: The Scorpion Pass (Akrabbim) is on the southern border of Judah, near Edom (Numbers 34:4; Joshua 15:3). An Amorite border there is strange, since the chapter has just placed the Amorites west of Benjamin. In Hebrew, "Amorite" ('emori) and "Edomite" ('edomi) differ mainly by the look-alike letters r and d. The A text of the Greek has both, "the Amorite, the Idumean," which looks like an early correction to "Edomite" copied in beside the old word; the B text has only "Amorite" (see the variant). Many commentators, from George Moore to Robert Boling, read "Edomites." "Sela" means "the rock" and may be a place in Edom (2 Kings 14:7). Others keep "Amorite" as a general name for the hill peoples, as in Joshua 24:15.

a: The angel of the LORD
p: The angel speaks as God himself: "I brought you up." Jewish tradition said he was a prophet, Phinehas.
b: Mal'akh means "messenger," and this one speaks in God's own voice. Leviticus Rabbah 1:1, followed by Rashi, says the messenger was Phinehas the priest, since prophets are also called messengers (Haggai 1:13), and the Targum makes him a prophet sent from the LORD. The Greek already points that way: the B text has him say "Thus says the Lord: I brought you up," and the A text "The Lord, the Lord brought you up," so that in both he quotes God rather than speaking as God (see the variant). Many modern scholars agree that a human messenger is possible here, because he "went up" from Gilgal on foot like a traveler. Others read him as the same figure who meets Gideon and Manoah (6:11–24; 13:3–23), the angel in whom God's name is (Exodus 23:20–21). Many Christian interpreters have seen in that figure the Son of God before his birth.

a: from Gilgal to Bochim
t: From Gilgal to the place of weeping
p: Gilgal was Israel's first camp in the land. Bochim, "weepers," was probably near Bethel.
b: Gilgal near Jericho was where Israel camped after crossing the Jordan, where it was circumcised and kept Passover (Joshua 4:19–5:12). The messenger's journey from Gilgal to Bochim is a journey away from the place of first faithfulness. Bochim is not mentioned anywhere else. The Septuagint adds "and to Bethel," and many scholars think Bochim was at or near Bethel, where an oak below the town was called Allon-bacuth, "oak of weeping" (Genesis 35:8). Israel gathers at Bethel to weep again in 20:26 and 21:2.

a: As for you, make no covenant with the people of this land.
p: The messenger repeats the commands of Exodus and Deuteronomy: no covenants, and tear down their altars.
b: These are the terms of the covenant at Sinai and in Moab: "Do not make a covenant with those who live in the land" (Exodus 34:15), and "Do not make a covenant with them, and do not show them mercy" (Deuteronomy 7:2), followed by "pull down their altars" (Deuteronomy 7:5; Exodus 34:13). Chapter 1 has just shown Israel making a deal at Bethel (1:24) and putting Canaanites to forced labor instead of driving them out. The question "What is this you have done?" echoes God's question to Eve in the garden (Genesis 3:13).

a: They will become barbs in your sides
p: The Hebrew says only "they will become sides for you." The word "barbs" is supplied from Numbers 33:55.
b: The Hebrew lakhem letsiddim means "to you for sides," which is too short to make sense alone. Numbers 33:55 warns that the people left in the land will become barbs (sikkim) in the eyes and thorns (tsninim) in the sides; the site's Plain English there has "barbs in your sides," and this verse borrows that phrase so the echo can be heard. Joshua 23:13 speaks of "a lash on your sides." Most translators borrow from those verses in the same way. The Greek and Latin read differently, "distresses" and "enemies," which may reflect a Hebrew word tsarim, "enemies" (see the variant). The "trap" (moqesh) is the word of Exodus 23:33: "you would serve their gods, and that would be a trap for you." Gideon's ephod becomes exactly that (8:27).

a: the people raised their voices in weeping
p: Israel weeps and sacrifices, but nothing in the story says the people changed.
b: The scene ends with tears and sacrifice, and the place is named for the weeping. The reader expects repentance, but 2:11–13 shows the same people serving the Baals. Many readers, Jewish and Christian, have taken Bochim as a picture of sorrow that stops short of turning back. Israel weeps again before God in this book at the war with Benjamin (20:23, 26) and for the lost tribe (21:2), each time when the damage is already done. Others read the weeping as sincere grief for a covenant broken, and the sacrifice as a real, if short-lived, return.

a: Joshua then let the people go
p: Verses 2:6–9 repeat Joshua 24:28–31 with small changes, to start the story over.
b: The wording follows Joshua 24: "Joshua then let the people go, and each of them went home to his own inheritance" (Joshua 24:28). The changes are telling. Joshua says the elders "knew all that the LORD had done for Israel" (Joshua 24:31); Judges says they "had seen" it, setting up the next generation, which "knew nothing of the LORD, or of the work he had done" (2:10). Judges also puts the verse about serving the LORD before Joshua's death, not after. Scholars call this kind of repeat a "resumptive repetition": the writer goes back to an earlier point in time to begin a new section, here the book's second introduction (2:6–3:6).

a: the servant of the LORD
p: 'Eved means servant or slave. "Servant of the LORD" is an honor title, given to Moses and then to Joshua.
b: The Hebrew 'eved covers everyone from a household slave to a king's minister; the Plain English chooses "servant" or "slave" by context. "Servant of the LORD" ('eved YHWH) is a title of honor. It is used again and again of Moses (Deuteronomy 34:5; Joshua 1:1), and Joshua receives it only at his death (Joshua 24:29). No judge in this book is called the LORD's servant. The title returns with David (2 Samuel 7:5) and the prophets.

a: Timnath-heres
p: Joshua 19:50 and 24:30 call the place Timnath-serah. Here the consonants are reversed: heres means "sun."
b: Joshua's town is Timnath-serah, "extra portion," in Joshua 19:50 and 24:30, and Timnath-heres, "portion of the sun," here. Many scholars think heres is the older name, tied to sun worship in the area (compare Mount Heres in 1:35 and Beth-shemesh, "house of the sun"), and that serah was a later change to avoid it. Others think the letters were simply switched by a scribe. Rashi explains the name from a legend that an image of the sun was set on Joshua's tomb in memory of the day the sun stood still (Joshua 10:12–13). The site is usually placed at Khirbet Tibnah, northwest of Bethel.

a: that knew nothing of the LORD, or of the work he had done for Israel
t: A generation that did not know
p: "Know" here means personal experience. The line echoes Pharaoh, "a king who did not know Joseph."
b: In Hebrew, to "know" (yada') the LORD is more than having heard of him. It is to have experienced his acts and to be bound to him in covenant (Hosea 4:1; Jeremiah 22:16). Deuteronomy made each parent responsible for teaching the next generation what God had done (Deuteronomy 6:6–7, 20–25). The line recalls Exodus 1:8, "a king who did not know Joseph," where forgetting began a long oppression. Many teachers, Jewish and Christian, have read this verse as a warning that faith does not pass to children on its own. "Gathered to its ancestors" is the common phrase for death and burial with one's family (Genesis 25:8).
r: Exodus 1:8; Deuteronomy 6:6–7; Deuteronomy 6:20–25; Psalm 78:4–8; Genesis 25:8; 1 Samuel 2:12

a: did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD
p: This line starts each judge's story. The book's last words turn it around: everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes.
b: "The Israelites did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD" opens the cycles at 3:7, 3:12, 4:1, 6:1, 10:6 and 13:1. The Plain English keeps "eyes" because the book ends with the reverse: "There was no king in Israel in those days. Everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes" (17:6; 21:25), the words Moses used for the time before the one chosen place (Deuteronomy 12:8). Samson too wants a woman because because she "is right in my eyes" (14:3). The question of Judges is whose eyes decide what is right, God's or each person's. The same phrase "evil in the eyes of the LORD" is used to judge every king in the books of Kings.
orig: וַיַּעֲשׂוּ ... אֶת־הָרַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה (vayya'asu ... et-hara' be'ene YHWH)

a: the Baals
p: Baal was the Canaanite storm god who was believed to bring rain. "The Baals" are his many local forms.
b: Ba'al means "lord, owner, husband." At Ugarit, a Canaanite city on the Syrian coast whose texts date to about 1300 BC, Baal is the storm god Hadad, who wins the kingship by defeating Sea and Death and who brings the rain that makes the fields grow. For farmers in the hills, the pull was obvious: Baal was the god of the harvest. The plural "Baals" refers to his many shrines and local names, such as Baal-berith at Shechem (8:33) and Baal-hermon (3:3). The LORD's claim that he, not Baal, sends rain and grain runs from Deuteronomy 11:13–17 to Elijah and Hosea.

a: the Ashtoreths
p: Ashtoreth is Astarte, a goddess of love and war. The Hebrew vowels may be a deliberate insult.
b: Astarte was worshiped across the Levant, especially at Sidon (1 Kings 11:5). Her name in Phoenician was probably 'Ashtart. Many scholars think the Hebrew writers gave it the vowels of boshet, "shame," to make 'Ashtoret, as they sometimes replaced "Baal" with "Bosheth" in names (Ishbaal becomes Ish-bosheth, 2 Samuel 2:8; compare 1 Chronicles 8:33). The plural "Ashtoreths," like "Baals," means the goddesses in general. Clay figurines of naked women, often linked with Astarte or Asherah, are common in Iron Age houses in Israel.

a: He sold them to the enemies around them
p: The picture is of a master selling a slave. It comes back in 3:8, 4:2, 4:9 and 10:7.
b: "Sell" (makhar) pictures Israel as a slave handed over for a price. The Song of Moses had asked how one enemy could chase a thousand Israelites "unless their Rock had sold them off" (Deuteronomy 32:30). Judges uses the verb at each new oppression (3:8; 4:2; 10:7) and then plays on it: "the LORD will sell Sisera into a woman's hands" (4:9). Later Isaiah answers that God "sold" Israel only because of its sins and will buy it back without money (Isaiah 50:1; Isaiah 52:3).

a: judges
p: A shofet in this book is a leader and rescuer, not mainly a courtroom judge.
b: The Hebrew shofet comes from shafat, "to judge, to set right, to rule." Only Deborah is shown deciding cases (4:4–5). The others lead armies, "rescue" Israel, and then "judge" it, meaning they govern. The word had this wider sense in the region: at Mari in Syria, officials called shapitum governed districts, and centuries later Carthage, a Phoenician colony, was led by two elected magistrates the Romans called sufetes. The book itself prefers the word "rescuer" (moshia', 3:9, 15). The title of the book in Hebrew is Shofetim, "Judges."

a: they went after other gods like a prostitute
p: The verb zanah pictures Israel as a wife who chases other lovers. It runs from Exodus to Hosea.
b: The Hebrew zanah, "act as a prostitute," treats the covenant with the LORD as a marriage and the worship of other gods as betrayal. Exodus 34:15–16 warns that the land's people "go chasing after their gods like prostitutes" and will lead Israel's sons to do the same, and Deuteronomy 31:16 predicts it. Judges uses the verb for Baal worship (2:17; 8:33) and for Gideon's ephod (8:27). Hosea, Jeremiah and Ezekiel build whole sermons on the picture (Hosea 1–3; Jeremiah 3; Ezekiel 16). Modern readers sometimes object that the image always makes the unfaithful partner female; others note that it was addressed to men as much as women.
orig: זָנוּ אַחֲרֵי אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים (zanu acharei elohim acherim)

a: The LORD was moved to pity by their groaning
p: The verb nicham means to be sorry, to relent or to be moved. God acts because of their pain, not their repentance.
b: Israel's groaning (ne'aqah) echoes Egypt, where "God heard their groans" (Exodus 2:24). The verb nicham is the one used when God "was sorry" he had made humankind (Genesis 6:6) or "changed his mind" about harm (Exodus 32:14). Here it means that God's pity moved him to act. Notice what the verse does not say: Israel does not repent before the judge comes. Many readers see this as pure mercy. Others point out that in the stories that follow, Israel's "crying out" is mostly a cry of pain, until 10:10–16 where God tests whether its confession is real.

a: Once the judge was dead, they would go back and behave worse than their ancestors
p: 2:11–19 sets out the book's pattern: sin, oppression, cry, rescue, rest. Each round is worse.
b: This paragraph gives the pattern of chapters 3–16: Israel does evil, God hands it to an enemy, Israel cries out, God raises a judge who rescues it, the land is quiet, and the judge dies. The Deuteronomistic History, the history from Deuteronomy to Kings that most scholars think was edited in the seventh and sixth centuries BC, uses such patterns to explain disaster as the result of unfaithfulness. But the pattern is not a flat circle. Each generation would "behave worse than their ancestors." Literary readers such as Webb, Exum and Block trace a downward spiral: the cycles break down, the judges grow more flawed, and by Samson the pattern hardly works. Traditional readers stress God's patience through it all (Nehemiah 9:26–28).

a: Through these nations I will test Israel
p: Judges gives three reasons: as punishment, as a test, and to teach war. Exodus gives a fourth: slowly, for Israel's good.
b: The text gives several reasons why Canaanites remained. They are punishment for disobedience (2:3, 20–21). They are a test of Israel's loyalty (2:22; 3:1, 4). They were left so later generations could learn war (3:2). Earlier books add a gentler reason: God would drive them out "bit by bit," so the land would not go wild (Exodus 23:29–30; Deuteronomy 7:22). Critical scholars often see several layers of editing here, each with its own explanation. Others see one author looking at the same fact from several sides. All agree that the land was not fully taken, which matches the archaeology of Canaanite towns surviving into the Iron Age.

a: so that the generations of Israel would come to know war
p: An odd reason: the new generations must learn to fight. Readers differ on what kind of "war" is meant.
b: The generation of Joshua had seen God fight for them. Their children had not. Some readers take the verse at face value: Israel had to learn to defend itself, and the remaining peoples gave it practice. Others, including many Jewish and Christian commentators, read "know war" in the light of 2:22: the generations were to learn that Israel's wars are won by obeying the LORD, not by numbers or weapons, which is the lesson of Gideon's three hundred (7:2). Critical scholars often think this verse is a later note giving a less moral reason than 2:20–22 and 3:4.

a: the five rulers of the Philistines
p: The Philistines' rulers had a special title, seren, which may be related to the Greek word tyrannos.
b: The Philistines settled on the southern coast of Canaan in the early twelfth century BC, part of the movement of the "Sea Peoples" that Egypt's Ramesses III fought around 1175 BC. Their five cities were Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath (Joshua 13:3; 1 Samuel 6:17). Each was led by a seren, a word used only for Philistine rulers. Many scholars link it to Greek tyrannos, "ruler," possibly through a language of western Anatolia. Their pottery, hearths and diet (including pork) point to roots in the Aegean world. In Judges they first appear briefly (3:31; 10:7) before becoming the main enemy in Samson's story.

a: They married those peoples' daughters
p: Intermarriage was forbidden with the peoples of the land because it led to serving their gods.
b: Deuteronomy 7:3 says, "Do not marry into their families. Do not give your daughters to their sons, and do not take their daughters for your sons." The reason follows at once: "they will turn your sons away from following me" (Deuteronomy 7:4). Judges reports the exact reverse, and the result. The concern in these laws is worship, not race: Rahab and Ruth married into Israel after joining its God (Joshua 6:25; Ruth 1:16). The problem comes back in Samson's marriage (14:1–3), in Solomon's (1 Kings 11:1–8), and after the exile (Ezra 9–10; Nehemiah 13:23–27).

a: the Baals and the Asherahs
p: Here the Hebrew says Asherahs; 2:13 and 10:6 say Ashtoreths. Some old translations read Ashtoreths here too.
b: Asherah was a mother goddess, wife of El at Ugarit, and her symbol was a wooden pole or living tree (6:25). The plural 'asherot here is unusual, because elsewhere the pair is "the Baals and the Ashtoreths" (2:13; 10:6; 1 Samuel 7:4). The Latin Vulgate reads "Ashtoreths," and some scholars think that is original. Others keep "Asherahs" as the harder reading. The KJV followed the Greek and Latin habit of rendering asherah as a "grove," which hides that a goddess is meant.

a: Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram-naharaim
p: The name means something like "dark Cushan, doubly wicked," probably a mocking nickname for a foreign king.
b: Rish'atayim means "double wickedness," a name no parent would give. Most scholars think it is a scornful nickname, with a rhyme on Aram-naharaim, "Aram of the two rivers," upper Mesopotamia. Some historians connect him with a Syrian ruler named in Egyptian texts of the twelfth century; Abraham Malamat proposed a usurper called Irsu. Others note that Othniel's home was in the far south, and that Cushan is a name tied to Midian and Edom (Habakkuk 3:7), so they read "Edom" ('edom) for "Aram" ('aram), two words that look alike in Hebrew. The story itself gives no details at all, which fits its role as a model cycle.

a: a rescuer
p: Moshia', "one who rescues," comes from the same root as the names Joshua, Hosea and Jesus.
b: The verb hoshia', "rescue, save, give victory," and the noun moshia' describe a person who brings people out of danger. In the Old Testament this saving is usually from enemies, sickness or trouble, not from sin. Nehemiah 9:27 sums up the period: "you gave them rescuers, and they rescued them from their foes' power." The same root is in Yehoshua (Joshua), Hoshea (Hosea), and Yeshua (Jesus). The KJV's "deliverer" and the older "savior" both stand for this one word.

a: Othniel had the Spirit of the LORD on him
p: The Spirit comes on Othniel, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson for a task. It does not make them good men.
b: The phrase "the Spirit of the LORD was on" (vattehi 'alav ruach YHWH) recurs with Jephthah (11:29), and the Spirit "clothes" Gideon (6:34) and "rushes" on Samson (14:6, 19; 15:14). In Judges the Spirit gives strength and courage for a crisis; it is not said to make anyone holy, and Gideon, Jephthah and Samson all fail badly after it comes. Jewish readers called this ruach gevurah, a spirit of might, as distinct from prophecy. Christian readers often contrast these temporary gifts with the Spirit poured out on all believers (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17). Othniel's story, the first and shortest, has the Spirit and no flaws: the model judge.

a: So the land was quiet for forty years.
p: The rests come in forties and eighties, round numbers that often mean a generation.
b: The periods of quiet are forty years (3:11; 5:31; 8:28) and eighty (3:30), and the oppressions are 8, 18, 20, 7 and 18 years. Forty is the Bible's number for a generation, as in the forty years in the wilderness. Some scholars think these are round symbolic numbers; others take them as real, with some judges overlapping in different regions. Added together, the years in Judges come to about 410, which is hard to fit into the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 together with Moses, Joshua, Eli, Samuel, Saul and David. For Jephthah's "three hundred years" see 11:26.

a: the LORD made Eglon king of Moab strong against Israel
p: The text says God himself made Moab strong. The oppressor is God's tool.
b: Judges does not treat the enemy as an accident. God "sells" Israel (2:14) and here "makes strong" (chizzeq) a foreign king. Isaiah will say the same of Assyria, "the rod of my anger" (Isaiah 10:5), and Jeremiah of Babylon (Jeremiah 27:6). Readers have long asked how God can use a cruel ruler and still judge him. The biblical answer is that the ruler is responsible for his own pride and cruelty (Isaiah 10:7–15), while God remains in control of the outcome. Eglon here gets no speech, no motive, and no say in his end.

a: they took possession of the City of Palms
p: The City of Palms is Jericho. Moab crossed the Jordan and held the oasis west of the river.
b: Jericho is called the City of Palms in Deuteronomy 34:3 and 2 Chronicles 28:15. Joshua had cursed anyone who rebuilt it as a walled town (Joshua 6:26), and Hiel later did so at the cost of his sons (1 Kings 16:34). But the oasis with its spring was always lived in, as the presence of David's envoys there shows (2 Samuel 10:5). Archaeologists have found only scant remains at Tell es-Sultan from this period. Moab, east of the Dead Sea, often pushed north into the plains across from Jericho, and its allies here, Ammon and Amalek, appear again as Israel's foes (6:3; 10:7).

a: the Benjaminite, a man hampered in his right hand
t: Left-handed, or bound in the right hand?
p: The Hebrew says his right hand was "bound." It may mean a disability or training to fight left-handed.
b: Itter yad-yemino means "bound" or "restricted" in his right hand. Some take it as a disability. Others, noting that Benjamin had seven hundred elite soldiers "bound in their right hand" who could sling a stone at a hair (20:16), and archers who could shoot with either hand (1 Chronicles 12:2), think it describes left-handers trained by binding the right arm in childhood. There is a pun as well: "Benjamin" means "son of the right hand." Either way, a right-handed guard would search a man's left thigh for a weapon, so Ehud's sword on his right thigh (3:16) went unnoticed.

a: tribute
p: The word for tribute, minchah, is also the word for an offering to God. The story plays on both.
b: Subject peoples sent yearly tribute to their overlord, often carried in a formal procession and presented at court; Assyrian palace reliefs show such scenes. The Hebrew minchah means a gift or tribute, and in worship it is the "grain offering" (Leviticus 2:1). Robert Alter and other literary readers note that the whole scene reads like a sacrifice: Eglon's name sounds like 'egel, "calf"; he is "fat" (bari'), a word used of fattened animals (1 Kings 4:23, "fattened oxen"); he receives a minchah; and the blade goes into his fat. The Moabite king is offered up.

a: a short cubit long
p: The measure, gomed, appears only here. It was probably shorter than a cubit, perhaps about a foot.
b: The Hebrew gomed occurs nowhere else. The Greek translators wrote "a span," about nine inches; most scholars think it was shorter than the regular cubit of about eighteen inches, perhaps a foot or a little more. The point is that the weapon was short enough to hide under a robe and long enough to kill. It was "two-mouthed," double-edged, a stabbing blade rather than a slashing sword. Daggers of about this length are known from Canaanite and Egyptian sites of the period.

a: Eglon was a very fat man.
p: Many readers find the Ehud story funny: the fat king, the locked toilet, the embarrassed servants.
b: The story is told with gross physical humor: Eglon is so fat the handle disappears; his servants wait outside the locked room thinking he is on the toilet; they wait "until they felt ashamed." Israelite listeners would have laughed at the Moabite oppressor. Literary readers such as Robert Alter and Lillian Klein see satire as a weapon here. Some readers are troubled by the deceit and the lack of any religious language (see the note at 3:21). Jewish tradition noted instead that Eglon rose from his throne at the mention of God (3:20) and was rewarded (see that note).

a: the carved stones by Gilgal
p: The word pesilim usually means carved idols. Here it may mark a border shrine, or the stones of Joshua 4.
b: Pesilim normally means "carved images" (Deuteronomy 7:5), and the KJV reads "quarries" here. The stones mark a spot near Gilgal where Ehud turned back, and again where he escaped (3:26), so they were a landmark, possibly a boundary between Moab's area and Israel's. Some have suggested they were the twelve stones Joshua set up at Gilgal (Joshua 4:20), now treated as idols. Others suggest Moabite statues marking the edge of Eglon's territory. The text does not explain, but the mention of idols just before Ehud's "word from God" may be deliberate.

a: I have a word from God for you.
p: Davar means both "word" and "thing." Ehud's "word from God" turns out to be a blade.
b: In 3:19 Ehud says he has a "secret word" (devar-seter); here, a "word of God" (devar-Elohim). Hebrew davar means "word, message, matter, thing," so both lines are double-edged, like the sword. Eglon stands, perhaps out of respect for a divine message. The Talmud cites Eglon's rising as a model of respect for God's word (Bavli Sanhedrin 60a). A midrash adds that God rewarded him: Ruth the Moabite, an ancestor of David, came from his line (Ruth Rabbah 2:9). The Talmud itself traces Ruth to Balak, Eglon's ancestor in its tradition (Bavli Nazir 23b). Christian readers have compared the "two-mouthed" sword with God's word, "sharper than any two-mouthed sword" (Hebrews 4:12).

a: drove it into his belly
p: Ehud kills a king by a trick, after using God's name to get him alone. Readers have both defended and judged him.
b: The defense: the LORD "raised up" Ehud as a rescuer (3:15), so the narrator presents him as God's agent, not a private murderer. Eglon was a foreign king holding Israel under tribute by force (3:12–14), and this was a war of liberation. Ancient Israel, like its neighbors, allowed deceit against an enemy in war, as with the Hebrew midwives (Exodus 1:15–21) and Rahab (Joshua 2:1–7). Calvin held that God at times raised up open avengers against tyrants, naming the judges among them, while denying that private persons may do the same (Institutes 4.20.30). The critique: Ehud gets Eglon alone by announcing "a word from God" (3:20) and then delivers a blade, using God's name as bait. The story never says God told him to do it, and no prayer or word from God is reported. Lillian Klein and Susan Niditch read the episode as trickster tale and ironic satire, not a model for conduct, and some modern readers see in its cunning the first sign of the moral slide the book goes on to trace.

a: And the waste came out.
t: A word nobody is sure of
p: Parshedonah occurs only here. It may mean the dung, the blade's tip, or a hole Ehud escaped through.
b: The last words read vayyetse happarshedonah, "and it/he went out the parshedon." There are three main readings. (1) The dung came out, as the dying man's bowels let go; this fits the servants' guess in 3:24 (the KJV's "the dirt came out"). (2) The blade came out at his back. (3) Ehud went out through the parshedon, some opening in the room. Baruch Halpern argued that the cool upper room had a toilet over a shaft, and that Ehud escaped down it, while the doors stayed locked from inside. The next verse has another rare word, misderonah, "porch" or "vestibule." The Plain English takes reading (1).

a: He must be covering his feet in the cool room
p: The Hebrew says "he is covering his feet," a polite way to say he was using the toilet.
b: The Hebrew mesikh hu et-raglav, "he is covering his feet," was a polite phrase for relieving oneself, since a man squatting in a long robe covered his feet. It is used again when Saul goes into a cave in 1 Samuel 24:3. The KJV kept it literally ("he covereth his feet"), and so does the Plain English, with a gloss giving the sense. The servants' guess, and the smell they would have noticed (3:22), give Ehud time to escape.

a: took control of the Jordan fords toward Moab
p: Seizing the fords cut off Moab's retreat. The same tactic comes back with Gideon and Jephthah, with a darker turn.
b: The Jordan could be crossed only at certain shallow places. By holding them, Ehud's men trapped the Moabites west of the river. Gideon uses the same tactic against Midian, with Ephraim's help (7:24). Then Jephthah's men hold the fords against Ephraim itself and kill those who cannot say "Shibboleth" (12:5–6). Literary readers see a pattern: the fords where Israel crossed into the land (Joshua 3) become a place where Israel traps first foreigners and finally its own brothers.

a: fat and strong
p: The word for the Moabite soldiers, "fat," echoes their fat king.
b: The Hebrew kol-shamen, "every fat one," means strong and well-fed, but it repeats the joke about Eglon, who was "very fat" (bari' me'od, 3:17). The well-fed soldiers fall like their well-fed king. Some translations hide the pun with "robust" or "able-bodied"; the Plain English keeps "fat." Moab's numbers, "about ten thousand," may be a round figure or a count of units (see 1:4).

a: Shamgar son of Anath
p: Anath was a Canaanite war goddess. Shamgar may have been a foreign fighter whose deed helped Israel.
b: Shamgar gets one verse and no "judged Israel" formula. His name may be Hurrian (the Hurrians were a people of northern Mesopotamia and Syria), and "son of Anath" recalls the warrior goddess of Ugarit, perhaps as the title of a fighting band, or the name of a town, Beth-anath (1:33). An ox goad was a long stick with a metal point for driving oxen (1 Samuel 13:21), a farmer's tool used as a weapon, like Samson's jawbone (15:15). The Song of Deborah dates its hard times to "the days of Shamgar son of Anath" (5:6). In some Greek manuscripts the Shamgar verse is repeated after Samson's story (16:31), where his fight with the Philistines also fits.

a: Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor
p: Joshua 11 already killed a Jabin of Hazor and burned the city. How can a Jabin rule there now?
b: Joshua 11:10–11 says Joshua "took Hazor, and he cut down its king with the sword," and burned it; that king was Jabin (Joshua 11:1). Excavations at Hazor, the largest Canaanite city in the land, by Yigael Yadin and later Amnon Ben-Tor, found a violent destruction by fire in the thirteenth century BC, after which the great city lay empty for a long time. Some traditional readers suggest "Jabin" was a dynastic name, like Pharaoh, and that Hazor's kingdom revived. Others think Judges 4 tells a battle that happened before Joshua's, or that two traditions about the same war were preserved. Many critical scholars think the name was added to Judges 4 from Joshua 11. Notably, the Song in chapter 5 never mentions Jabin or Hazor.

a: Harosheth-haggoyim
p: The name means "Harosheth of the nations" or "the forest of the nations." Its site is unknown.
b: Sisera's base was somewhere near the Kishon River and the Jezreel Valley. No town by this name has been found, and some scholars think charoshet means a wooded area or worked farmland rather than a city, "the farmland of the nations" in the western Jezreel. "Of the nations" (haggoyim) suggests a mixed population, as in "Galilee of the nations" (Isaiah 9:1). Sisera's name is not Semitic and may be connected with the Sea Peoples or with Luwian names (Luwian was a language of southern Anatolia), though this is uncertain.

a: Deborah, a woman and a prophet
p: Deborah is called a prophet, a judge and "woman of Lappidoth," which may mean "fiery woman."
b: Deborah means "bee." She is ishah nevi'ah, "a woman, a prophet," like Miriam (Exodus 15:20), Huldah (2 Kings 22:14) and Isaiah's wife (Isaiah 8:3). Eshet lappidot is usually taken as "wife of Lappidoth," but no husband ever appears, and lappidot means "torches." Some read "a woman of fire," a spirited woman. The Talmud says she made wicks for the sanctuary lamps (Bavli Megillah 14a). The commander she calls is Barak, "Lightning," which makes a striking pair with "torches." She is the only judge whose story begins with her already judging.
orig: אִשָּׁה נְבִיאָה אֵשֶׁת לַפִּידוֹת (ishah nevi'ah eshet lappidot)

a: was the one judging Israel at that time
p: Readers have argued for centuries about what Deborah's leadership means for women's roles.
b: The Hebrew stresses "she" (hi') as the one judging. The rabbis honored her as one of Israel's seven women prophets (Bavli Megillah 14a), yet they also criticized her for summoning Barak instead of going to him, and for praising herself in her song (Bavli Megillah 14b; Bavli Pesachim 66b, on 5:7). Some Christian commentators, from the Reformers on, held that God raised her up because the men of her day failed, an exception rather than a pattern. Others, Jewish and Christian, see her as a model of God calling women to lead. Feminist scholars note both her authority and the way the story still channels the final glory to Jael. The text itself states her role without comment.

a: She used to sit beneath Deborah's Palm
p: Leaders often judged in the open, at a gate or under a well-known tree. Deborah's palm stood in the hills of Ephraim.
b: In the ancient Near East, cases were heard at the town gate (Ruth 4:1–2) or at a landmark tree (1 Samuel 22:6, Saul under a tamarisk). Deborah sat between Ramah and Bethel, the same area where Samuel later judged (1 Samuel 7:15–17). Genesis tells of another Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, buried under an oak below Bethel, called the "oak of weeping" (Genesis 35:8). Some scholars think the two traditions came together around a famous tree near Bethel. "Came up to her for judgment" may mean ordinary legal cases or requests for a word from God; as a prophet she may have given both.

a: Go, draw your men toward Mount Tabor
p: The same verb, mashakh, is used for Barak drawing his men and God drawing Sisera.
b: God tells Barak, "draw" (meshokh) toward Tabor, and then says, "I will draw" (umashakhti) Sisera to the Kishon. The repeated verb shows the plan: Israel gathers on the mountain, God lures the chariots into the wet valley below. Mount Tabor is a steep, rounded hill rising about 1,300 feet above the northeast edge of the Jezreel Valley, where the territories of Zebulun, Naphtali and Issachar met (Joshua 19:12, 22, 34). Chariots could not climb it. Kedesh in Naphtali was Barak's home town, probably the Kedesh near the Sea of Galilee rather than the one in upper Galilee.

a: the Kishon River
p: The Kishon drains the Jezreel Valley to the sea near Haifa. Most of the year it is a small stream; after rain it floods.
b: The Hebrew nachal means a valley with a stream that runs mainly in the rainy season, a wadi. The Kishon gathers water from the Jezreel Valley and flows west past Megiddo and Taanach to the Bay of Haifa. In a winter storm it can rise fast and turn the clay plain to mud, which would make chariots useless. The Song says exactly this happened: "The Kishon River swept them away" (5:21). Elijah later killed Baal's prophets at the Kishon (1 Kings 18:40), and Psalm 83:9 remembers Sisera and Jabin "at the wadi Kishon."

a: If you go with me, I will go.
p: Is Barak a coward, or a man of faith who wants God's prophet beside him? Readers are split.
b: Many readers see weakness: Barak will not obey God's command without a woman to hold his hand, and so loses the glory (4:9). Others read his request as faith: a prophet carried God's word and presence, as the ark or a priest did, and Barak wanted God's word at hand in battle. The Septuagint adds a reason that supports this second reading: "for I do not know the day when the LORD will give his angel success with me" (see the variant). Hebrews 11:32 lists Barak, not Deborah, among the heroes of faith, and 1 Samuel 12:11 in the Greek names Barak among Israel's rescuers.

a: the LORD will sell Sisera into a woman's hands
p: The reader assumes Deborah. The surprise is Jael.
b: Deborah's word sounds like a rebuke to Barak and a promise of her own glory. But the woman who kills Sisera is Jael, an outsider whom the reader has not met. The verb "sell" picks up 4:2: God sold Israel to Jabin; now he sells Jabin's general to a woman. Ancient warriors counted death at a woman's hand as the worst shame, as Abimelech's last words show (9:54). Literary readers note that the book's first three heroines, Achsah, Deborah and Jael, all act with more courage than the men around them.

a: Heber the Kenite
t: Heber, the Kenite who moved north
p: Heber's clan had left the other Kenites in the south and pitched tents near Kedesh. He was at peace with Jabin.
b: The Kenites lived with Judah in the south (1:16). Heber, whose name may mean "companion" or "ally," had split off and moved north near Kedesh. Hobab is here called Moses' father-in-law (compare Numbers 10:29, where he is the son of Reuel, Moses' father-in-law; the Hebrew word can mean any male in-law). Kenites may have worked as smiths, which would explain good relations with a king who needed iron for nine hundred chariots (4:17). The verse is placed here to prepare for Sisera's flight to Heber's tent, and its note of the treaty makes Jael's act a betrayal of her husband's ally.

a: the LORD threw Sisera into panic
p: Hamam, "throw into panic," is the verb of the Red Sea and of Joshua's battle at Gibeon.
b: At the sea the LORD "threw Egypt's camp into confusion" (Exodus 14:24), and at Gibeon "the LORD sent them into confusion in front of Israel" (Joshua 10:10). The same verb is used for Samuel's victory, when God thundered against the Philistines (1 Samuel 7:10). It belongs to the language of holy war: God, not Israel's army, breaks the enemy. The prose says only that God caused panic; the Song adds the stars fighting and the Kishon in flood (5:20–21), which suggests a storm. Sisera's leaving his chariot to run on foot (4:15, 17) fits a battlefield turned to mud.

a: Turn aside to me. Do not be afraid.
p: Jael breaks the duty of a host to protect a guest. Was she a heroine, a traitor or both?
b: In the ancient Near East a guest under one's roof was sacred; Lot offered his daughters rather than hand over his guests (Genesis 19:8). Jael invites Sisera in, covers him and gives him milk, and then kills him. For the Song she is "blessed above women" (5:24). The rabbis praised her deed as a sin done for the sake of heaven, greater than a commandment done for its own sake (Bavli Nazir 23b; Bavli Horayot 10b). Many modern readers are uneasy with her deceit. Others point out that a woman alone could not refuse a fleeing general, that he broke custom by entering a woman's tent, and that she chose Israel's side over her husband's treaty. Her motive is never stated.

a: She opened the skin of milk
p: He asks for water and gets milk, more than he asked, a host's generosity that also makes a tired man sleep.
b: Milk was kept in goatskin bags and was often soured or churned into a thick drink, still common among Bedouin. The Song calls it "cream" or "curds" served in a fine bowl (5:25). Josephus says she gave him milk that had already turned. The point in the prose is that Jael gives more than he asked and covers him twice, playing the mother, so that he trusts her completely before she strikes.

a: drove the peg into his temple until it went down into the ground
p: In Bedouin custom women pitched the tents, so Jael used tools she handled every day.
b: Pitching and striking tents was women's work among tent-dwellers, so a tent peg and a wooden mallet were at hand and familiar to her. The verb for the peg going "down into the ground" is tsanach, the rare word used for Achsah getting down from her donkey (1:14). The prose says Sisera was asleep and worn out; the Song pictures him standing and then sinking at her feet (5:27). The last Hebrew words, vayya'af vayyamot, can be read "he was exhausted, and he died," or with a different reading of the first verb, "he twitched and died."

a: until they had cut Jabin king of Canaan off
p: Chapter 4 tells the battle in prose, chapter 5 in poetry. They differ in details, as two witnesses often do.
b: Like the Red Sea (Exodus 14 and 15), this victory is told twice. The prose names Jabin, two tribes, a sleeping Sisera and a tent peg through the temple. The Song names ten tribes, praises some and shames others, adds the storm and flood, has Sisera struck while drinking, and ends in his mother's window. Many scholars think the Song is older, perhaps from the twelfth or eleventh century BC, and the prose was written later partly from it. Traditional readers see the two as complementary, one giving events, the other their meaning. Either way, the doubling invites the reader to compare and to notice what each one stresses.

a: Then Deborah sang on that day
t: One of the oldest poems in the Bible
p: Many scholars date the Song of Deborah to the twelfth or eleventh century BC, close to the events.
b: The Song's Hebrew is unusually old. It uses word forms and spellings found in the Ugarit texts and rarely elsewhere in the Bible, such as the relative particle she- (5:7) and verbs with archaic endings. Its picture of Israel, a loose league of tribes without Judah, with no king or central shrine, fits the early Iron Age. For these reasons many scholars, including W. F. Albright, Frank Moore Cross and David Noel Freedman, counted it among the earliest Hebrew poems, with the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15). Others date it later, arguing that old forms can be imitated. The verb "sang" is feminine singular: Deborah leads, and Barak joins.

a: When hair flies loose in Israel
p: The opening words are disputed. They may describe warriors with long, unbound hair, or leaders taking the lead.
b: Bifroa' pera'ot repeats one root. Pera' means long, loose hair in Numbers 6:5, where a Nazirite "lets the hair on his head grow long," and Deuteronomy 32:42 speaks of "the heads of the enemy's princes," a phrase some read as "long-haired heads." Warriors who had vowed themselves to holy war may have let their hair hang loose, as Samson the Nazirite did. Others, citing an Arabic word for "be first," read "when leaders lead." The Greek manuscripts already disagreed (see the variant). The Plain English keeps the hair, the more concrete reading.

a: O LORD, as you came out of Seir
p: The LORD marches from Seir and Edom, south of Israel. Several old poems picture him coming from there.
b: Seir is the mountain country of Edom, south and east of the Dead Sea. Moses' blessing says, "The LORD came from Sinai / and rose like the dawn over them from Seir" (Deuteronomy 33:2), and Habakkuk 3:3 has God coming from Teman and Mount Paran. Psalm 68:7–8 repeats this verse and the next almost word for word. Inscriptions found at Kuntillet Ajrud in the Sinai, from about 800 BC, bless people by "Yahweh of Teman." Many historians take these texts as evidence that Israel's God was first worshiped in the southern deserts, near Midian and Edom. The earthquake and storm are the signs of his coming to fight for his people.

a: Mountains ran like water
p: The verb can mean "flowed" or "quaked." The Greek read "shook."
b: The Hebrew nazelu looks like a form of nazal, "flow, stream," the word used for water in 5:4 and Exodus 15:8. The Septuagint read it as "were shaken," from a similar root zalal. Isaiah 64:1 uses the same word: "so the mountains would shake (or flow) in front of you." Both pictures fit a storm theophany, an appearance of God in storm: mountains running with rain, or rocking in an earthquake. The Plain English keeps the water image, which continues the dripping skies of 5:4.

a: the One of Sinai
p: The Hebrew zeh Sinai may be an old title for God: "the One of Sinai," "Lord of Sinai."
b: Read as normal Hebrew, zeh Sinai means "this Sinai," which makes little sense in Seir. Many scholars since Albright have compared Ugaritic and Arabic, where a word like zeh/dhu means "the one of, lord of," and read "the One of Sinai." Psalm 68:8 has the same phrase. The older reading takes it as a pointer, "even Sinai," meaning that Sinai itself trembled, as it did when God came down on it (Exodus 19:18). Either way, the God who fights for the tribes is the God of Sinai and the covenant.

a: the caravans stopped
p: Under Canaanite control the trade routes were unsafe, so travelers kept to back paths.
b: The Hebrew orachot can mean "roads" or "caravans," the traveling trade groups that moved along the main routes (Genesis 37:25; Job 6:19). The great road through the Jezreel Valley was controlled by fortified towns. Israelites in the hills could not use it safely, so trade stopped and travelers took winding paths. Lawrence Stager argued that the Song reflects the economy of hill villages cut off from the lowland roads and ports. Shamgar (3:31) and Jael are named as markers of the time, much as one might say "in the days of a certain governor."

a: Village life stopped in Israel
p: The rare word perazon may mean villagers, open country, or fighting men. Each changes the picture.
b: Perazon appears here and in 5:11, and a related word, perazi, means people of open, unwalled villages (Deuteronomy 3:5; 1 Samuel 6:18). So most read "village life" or "villagers" ceased: people fled the farms. Others connect it with an Arabic word for "champion" and read "the warriors were gone," which fits the lack of shield and spear in 5:8. The Greek translators guessed "the mighty" or "the rulers." Archaeology shows hundreds of small unwalled villages in the hills at this period, the earliest Israelite settlements, which gives the first reading real force.

a: till I rose up, Deborah
p: The verb form qamti can be first person, "I arose," or an old second-person form, "you arose."
b: In later Hebrew qamti means "I arose," so Deborah speaks of herself. But in older Hebrew, as in Ugaritic, the same form could be second person feminine, "you arose," and 5:12 does address her: "Up, up, Deborah!" Many scholars therefore read "until you arose, Deborah." The rabbis took it as first person and saw pride in it: when Deborah praised herself, her prophetic spirit left her for a time (Bavli Pesachim 66b). "A mother in Israel" is a title of honor for a woman whose wisdom protects a community, like the wise woman of Abel (2 Samuel 20:19).

a: They chose new gods
t: New gods, or God chose new men?
p: The line can mean Israel chose new gods, or God chose new leaders. Each fits a different reading of the song.
b: Yivchar elohim chadashim can be read "they chose new gods" (the most common reading, echoing "new gods" in Deuteronomy 32:17) or "God chose new ones," new leaders like Deborah and Barak. The Targum paraphrases: when Israel chose to serve new idols, war came upon them. The next line is also hard: az lachem she'arim may mean "then war was at the gates," or with different vowels "then barley bread" (lechem), which the Greek seems to have read. The question of 5:8b fits the first reading: Israel's idolatry left it disarmed. The Philistines later kept Israel from making weapons (1 Samuel 13:19–22).

a: You who ride on tawny donkeys
p: The verse calls on everyone, from nobles on fine donkeys to people on foot, to tell the story.
b: Donkeys were the mounts of important people in this period; Jair's and Abdon's sons ride them as a sign of rank (10:4; 12:14), and Zechariah's king comes riding on one (Zechariah 9:9). "Tawny" (tsechorot) probably means light-colored, reddish-white. Middin may be saddle blankets or rugs. The three groups, riders, sitters and walkers, together mean the whole people, rich and poor. The verb sichu can mean "tell" or "think about": consider what God has done and talk about it.

a: there they retell the LORD's just deeds
p: Tsidqot, "righteous acts," means the times God set things right by saving his people.
b: Tsidqot YHWH are acts of the LORD's righteousness, which in a poem like this means his victories for his people, setting right what was wrong (1 Samuel 12:7; Micah 6:5). The first line is uncertain: mechatsetsim has been read as "archers," "singers," or "those who share out water," from a root meaning "divide." The picture seems to be the village well, where people gathered to draw water and swap news, and where the story of the battle was told. The same verb, "retell" (tannah), describes the yearly mourning for Jephthah's daughter (11:40). In Judges, some stories are retold as praise and some as lament.

a: Then the survivors marched down to the nobles
p: The Hebrew of 5:13 is hard to follow, and translations differ widely.
b: With the vowels of the Masoretic Text the line reads roughly, "Then he made a remnant rule over the nobles; the LORD made me rule over the mighty." Most scholars repoint the verbs as yarad, "went down," as the Plain English does, to match the march down from the hills that the next verses describe. The Greek translators already struggled, and the two main Greek text forms differ here. The sense in any case is that the few who were left came down to face a stronger enemy, with the LORD's help.
orig: אָז יְרַד שָׂרִיד לְאַדִּירִים (az yerad sarid le'addirim)

a: whose root is in Amalek
p: Part of Ephraim's land was called the hill country of the Amalekites (12:15).
b: The Hebrew "from Ephraim, their root in Amalek" is hard. The simplest explanation is geographic: Abdon was buried "in the hill country of the Amalekites" in Ephraim (12:15), so some of Ephraim lived in an area named for Amalekites who had once been there. Others emend "in Amalek" to "in the valley" (ba'emeq), a small change of letters that the Greek seems to support. The line "Benjamin came behind you" may echo an old battle cry, "Behind you, Benjamin!" (Hosea 5:8).

a: From Machir came down commanders
p: The Song names ten tribes, praises six and shames four. Judah, Simeon and Levi are missing.
b: Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun, Issachar and Naphtali come (5:14–15, 18). Reuben, Gilead, Dan and Asher stay home (5:15–17). Machir is a clan of Manasseh (Numbers 32:39), and Gilead stands where we expect Gad. Judah and Simeon are not named at all. Critical historians use the list as evidence for an early Israel that was a loose federation of northern tribes, before the classic twelve-tribe list took shape. Traditional readers note that the southern tribes may have been too far away or cut off, and that the poem judges only those it expected to come. Either way, the Song shows that unity was a choice, not a given.

a: great were the plans of the heart
p: 5:15 and 5:16 play on two words: Reuben made great "resolutions" but then did great "heart-searching."
b: The poet uses a pun. In 5:15 Reuben's clans had chiqqeqe-lev, "decrees of the heart," great resolves. In 5:16 they had chiqre-lev, "searchings of the heart," endless deliberation. One letter changes. The picture is a tribe that talked and planned and never came. Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, lived east of the Dead Sea and was fading by this time (Genesis 49:3–4; Deuteronomy 33:6). Preachers have long used the line against good intentions that never become action.

a: between the saddlebags
p: Mishpetayim may mean saddlebags, sheepfolds or campfires. The same word is used of Issachar in Genesis 49:14.
b: The dual noun mishpetayim appears only here and in Genesis 49:14, where Issachar is a strong donkey "stretched out between the two folds." It may mean the two packs on a donkey's back, two walls of a sheep pen, or a pair of hearths. Either way the scene is pastoral and lazy: Reuben stayed with his flocks, listening to the shepherds' pipes, while others risked their lives. The sheriqot are whistlings or pipings used to call sheep.

a: And Dan, why did he hang around the ships?
p: Dan near the sea may have worked for coastal shipowners. Some scholars link Dan to a Sea People called the Denyen.
b: Before Dan moved north (chapter 18), its land reached toward the coast near Joppa (Joshua 19:46). The verb yagur means "live as a foreigner," which suggests Danites working for others on ships or at ports. Asher lived on the northern coast (Genesis 49:13 says the same of Zebulun). Yigael Yadin proposed that Dan was originally one of the Sea Peoples, the Denyen named in Egyptian records, who later joined Israel; most scholars find the evidence thin. The simpler point of the line is shame: these tribes cared more for trade than for their brothers.

a: Zebulun was a people who threw their lives away to the death
p: Zebulun and Naphtali, the two tribes Barak called (4:6, 10), bore the brunt of the battle.
b: The Hebrew cherref nafsho lamut means "scorned its life to death," risked everything. These are the two tribes named in the prose (4:6, 10), and Isaiah later names their land, "the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali," as the first to see a great light after darkness (Isaiah 9:1–2), a text Matthew applies to Jesus' work in Galilee (Matthew 4:13–16). "The high fields" may refer to the slopes of Tabor or the hills above the battle.

a: at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo
p: Two Canaanite towns at the southwest edge of the Jezreel Valley, five miles apart, by the Kishon's tributaries.
b: Taanach and Megiddo guarded the passes from the coast into the Jezreel Valley; both are on the list of towns Manasseh did not take (1:27). "The waters of Megiddo" are the streams that feed the Kishon. The kings fought for plunder, and "no silver did they carry off": they came to loot and went home with nothing. Megiddo, guarding the main pass, saw so many battles that its name became "Armageddon," the mountain of Megiddo, in Revelation 16:16.

a: The stars fought from heaven
p: The stars fight as God's army. Many readers take this as a poetic way to describe a storm.
b: In the ancient world the stars were often thought of as heavenly powers or soldiers, the "host of heaven" (Deuteronomy 4:19; Job 38:7). Here they fight for Israel "from their highways," the paths they travel across the sky. Many readers link the line to the rain: in Canaanite thought rain came from the heavens and its powers, and here the God of Israel commands them. Josephus tells the battle with a great storm of rain and hail that blew into the Canaanites' faces. Others read the stars as angels, the LORD's army (Joshua 5:14).

a: The Kishon River swept them away
p: A sudden flood of the Kishon turned the plain to mud and swept the chariots away.
b: The verb garaf means "sweep away" as a flood does. The Kishon is often a trickle, but winter rains can make it a torrent in hours. Many scholars think the battle came with an unexpected storm, perhaps out of season, which made the chariots worse than useless, as Egypt's chariots were at the sea (Exodus 14:25). "Tread on, my soul, with strength!" is the singer urging herself on, or, with a small change, a cry to trample "the strong" underfoot.

a: Curse Meroz
p: Meroz is a town known only from this verse. It is cursed for refusing to help.
b: No town called Meroz is known, and its site is lost, perhaps because the curse worked. It was probably an Israelite town near the battle that held back. The curse comes from "the angel of the LORD," and the reason is striking: they did not come "to the LORD's aid." The war is God's, and staying out is taking sides against him. The rabbis read the curse as a warning to bystanders. Some Christian preachers have used the verse against neutrality in moral struggles.

a: Blessed above women be Jael
p: The same blessing is given to Judith and, in Luke, to Mary.
b: "Blessed above women" (tevorakh minnashim) is high praise. In the book of Judith, which Catholic and Orthodox Christians include in the Old Testament, Uzziah tells Judith that the Most High God has blessed her above all the women on earth (Judith 13:18), a clear echo of Jael. Like Jael, Judith kills an enemy general who lies helpless in his tent (Judith 13:2–8), and her song says God beat the enemy "by a woman's hand" (Judith 16:5). In Luke, Elizabeth greets Mary with "Blessed are you among women" (Luke 1:42). Christian writers have seen Jael, who crushed the enemy's head, as a type of Mary and of the promise that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15). "Women in the tent" means women of the nomad camps.

a: Between her feet he bent down, he fell, he lay
p: The poem slows the death to a crawl. Many readers hear sexual overtones, and the rabbis drew on them.
b: The repeated verbs, "bent down," "fell," "lay," act out Sisera's collapse. "Between her feet" can refer to a woman's legs, and the verb kara' is used of a man bending over a woman in Job 31:10. Many literary readers, such as Robert Alter and Susan Niditch, see Jael reversing the expected roles: the man who came to take women as plunder (5:30) lies at a woman's feet. The rabbis went further and said Sisera lay with her seven times that day, counting the verbs (Bavli Nazir 23b; Bavli Yevamot 103a), which shows they read the line sexually. The prose says he was asleep (4:21); the poem seems to picture him standing and falling.

a: From the window she looked down and wailed
p: The scene of a woman looking out a window is a known image in the Bible and in Phoenician art.
b: The poem moves from Jael's tent to a palace window in Sisera's home. Ivory plaques found at Nimrud and Samaria show a woman's face framed in a window, a well-known image in Phoenician art. In the Bible, Michal watches David from a window (2 Samuel 6:16) and Jezebel looks down at Jehu just before her death (2 Kings 9:30). Sisera's mother waits for a son who will not come. Many readers feel sympathy for her; others see the poet's sharpest irony in what her ladies say next (5:30).

a: A womb or two for every man
p: The Hebrew says "a womb, two wombs." It is a crude word for captured girls, the plunder Sisera's men expected.
b: Racham rachamatayim literally means "a womb, two wombs." Ancient inscriptions from Moab use the same word for female captives (the Mesha Stele, about 840 BC). The ladies imagine the soldiers dividing up girls and dyed cloth. The poet lets the enemy's own women describe the sexual violence of war, and the reader already knows that Sisera lies dead at a woman's feet. Many translations soften the word to "a girl or two" or "a damsel," which hides how blunt the line is. The verse is one of the Bible's frankest descriptions of what conquest meant for women.

a: And may those who love him be like the sun
p: The Song ends with the LORD's friends rising like the sun. The image returns in Samuel, Malachi and Matthew.
b: The last line contrasts the enemies who perish with "those who love him," the covenant word of Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy 7:9). The image of the sun that "goes out in its strength" appears in David's last words about a just ruler, like the morning light (2 Samuel 23:4), in Malachi's "sun of righteousness" (Malachi 4:2), and in Jesus' saying that the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom (Matthew 13:43). Some Christian writers read the line as pointing to Christ, the rising sun.
