a: And the land was quiet for forty years.
p: The Song ends with the line before this one. The narrator's prose returns with the cycle's closing formula.
b: This sentence is not part of the poem. It is the narrator's formula that closes each rescue story (3:11; 3:30; 8:28), and it ends the Deborah story of chapters 4–5 as a whole. The Plain English keeps it on the verse's line because the verse is a single unit in the Hebrew, but it should be read as prose.
orig: וַתִּשְׁקֹט הָאָרֶץ אַרְבָּעִים שָׁנָה (vattishqot ha'arets arba'im shanah)

a: handed them over to Midian for seven years
p: Numbers 31 says Israel killed every Midianite man. Here Midian is a great power. Readers explain this in several ways.
b: In Numbers 31 Israel went to war against Midian "and they killed every male" (Numbers 31:7). A few generations later Midian invades with camels "past counting." Traditional readers note that Midian was a large federation of desert clans, and that Numbers 31 dealt with one group of them in Moab (Numbers 25:6, 15), so others survived. Ancient war reports, Israel's included, often speak of total destruction in sweeping terms. Critical scholars see separate traditions from different times. The book also echoes Moses: Moses fled to Midian and found a wife there; Gideon will be called, as Moses was, to rescue Israel from it.

a: the Israelites made themselves dens in the mountains
p: The limestone hills are full of caves. Israelites hid there from raiders, as they would from the Philistines.
b: The rare word minharot may mean holes, clefts or tunnels. The hills of central Israel are limestone, full of natural caves, and these served as shelters and storehouses in times of danger. In Saul's day, too, the people "hid themselves: in caves, in thorn bushes, among the cliffs, in underground rooms and in cisterns" (1 Samuel 13:6), and David hid in the caves of Adullam and En-gedi (1 Samuel 22:1; 1 Samuel 24:3). For a farming people, hiding meant leaving fields and harvests to the raiders, the very thing 6:3–4 describes.

a: the people of the East
p: "People of the East" (bene qedem) were the desert peoples east of the Jordan, like Job's countrymen.
b: The bene qedem were the tribes of the Syrian and Arabian deserts east of Israel (Genesis 29:1; Job 1:3; Isaiah 11:14). With Midian and Amalek they came at harvest time, when the grain was in the fields, and drove their herds over the crops. This is the classic pattern of nomad raids on farmland, attested in many periods. They swept all the way west to Gaza (6:4), which means they crossed the whole land through the Jezreel Valley.

a: Neither they nor their camels could be counted
p: This is the first camel-mounted raid in the Bible. Domestic camels became common in the land around 1000 BC.
b: Camels allowed desert tribes to cover great distances and to strike far from their home grounds. Studies of camel bones in the Aravah valley, by Lidar Sapir-Hen and Erez Ben-Yosef, suggest that domestic camels came into regular use in the southern Levant in the late tenth century BC, though earlier wild or occasional use is known. Some scholars therefore think the camel detail reflects the writer's own day. Others note that camels were known in Arabia earlier and that raiders from there may well have used them sooner. The camels' gold crescents (8:21, 26) show their riders' wealth.

a: the LORD sent a prophet to the Israelites
p: Before sending a rescuer, God sends a prophet with a rebuke. The Dead Sea Scroll 4QJudg-a lacks these verses.
b: The text calls him ish navi, "a man, a prophet," with no name. His speech uses the opening of the Ten Words, "I am the LORD your God" and the "house of slaves" (Exodus 20:2; Deuteronomy 5:6), and ends with the charge "you have not listened to my voice," with no promise of help. Many critical scholars see 6:7–10 as an editor's addition in the style of Deuteronomy, and point out that 4QJudg-a, a scroll from Qumran, goes straight from 6:6 to 6:11 (see the variants). Others think the scroll's scribe skipped the passage, or that it was left out of a shorter text. In either case, the book now has Israel cry out and receive first a sermon, then a savior.

a: the oak at Ophrah
p: Gideon's town was in Manasseh. It is not the Ophrah of Benjamin, and its site is unknown.
b: Abiezer was a clan of Manasseh (Joshua 17:2). Their Ophrah was probably in the hills west of the Jezreel Valley, though no site is certain; it is different from the Ophrah in Benjamin (Joshua 18:23). The "oak" or terebinth (elah) belonged to Joash, Gideon's father, who also owned an altar to Baal (6:25). A great tree beside an altar was a common feature of local shrines (Genesis 12:6–7; Hosea 4:13). The angel sits under the very tree linked with the family's Baal worship.

a: Gideon was beating out wheat in the winepress
p: Wheat was threshed on an open, windy floor. Gideon hides in a winepress pit, beating a little grain by hand.
b: Grain was normally threshed on a flat floor in an open, windy place, where oxen or sledges broke the heads and the wind blew the chaff away (Ruth 3:2). A winepress was a pit cut in rock where grapes were trodden, sheltered and out of sight. Gideon is "beating" (chovet) the wheat with a stick, as one did with small amounts (Ruth 2:17). The scene shows both his fear and the hunger of the times. The name Gideon probably means "hacker" or "one who cuts down," which he will do to Baal's altar.

a: you mighty fighter
t: Mighty fighter, or man of standing?
p: Gibbor hechayil can mean a brave warrior or a man of wealth and standing. Spoken to Gideon in hiding, it sounds ironic.
b: Gibbor chayil is used of warriors (11:1, Jephthah; Joshua 1:14) and of men of property and standing, like Boaz, "a man of great worth" (Ruth 2:1; compare 2 Kings 15:20). Gideon's family owned servants and an altar (6:25–27), so he may have been well-off. But spoken to a man hiding his wheat, the title is either irony or a promise: this is what God will make of him. Many preachers, Jewish and Christian, have read it as God calling a person by what he will become.

a: but if the LORD is with us, why has all this found us?
p: Gideon answers the greeting with a protest: if God is with us, why are we suffering? The Psalms ask the same.
b: Gideon takes the angel's "you" as "us" and asks the question of many lament psalms: where are the old wonders now (Psalm 44:1–24; Psalm 77:7–11)? His protest is honest, and the LORD does not rebuke it. But the reader knows the answer he has missed: the prophet just said why (6:7–10), and Gideon's own father keeps an altar to Baal. Rashi, following a midrash, reads "Go with this strength you have" (6:14) as praise: Gideon's strength was that he spoke up for his people before God. Others see in his words the doubt that runs through his whole story.

a: The LORD turned to face him
p: The text moves from "the angel of the LORD" to "the LORD" without a break.
b: In 6:11–12 the speaker is "the angel of the LORD"; in 6:14 and 6:16 it is simply "the LORD"; in 6:20 "the angel of God"; and in 6:22–23 Gideon realizes he has seen the angel face to face, and "the LORD" answers him. The same shift happens at the burning bush (Exodus 3:2–6). Some readers think the messenger speaks with God's full authority, like an ambassador. Others see a visible form of God himself. Many Christian interpreters, from Justin Martyr on, identified him as the Son of God before his birth. Some critical scholars think "angel of" was added in places by scribes uneasy with God appearing directly. The Greek shows that process at work: both the A and B texts read "the angel of the Lord" in 6:14 and 6:16, and in 6:16 the angel says "the Lord will be with you" instead of "I will be with you" (see the variant). In 6:23 the Greek keeps "the Lord."

a: my clan is the poorest in Manasseh
p: Gideon's call follows the pattern of Moses' call: an objection, a promise "I will be with you," and a sign.
b: Moses answered God's call with "Who am I to go to Pharaoh?" (Exodus 3:11), and God answered, "I will be with you" and gave a sign (Exodus 3:12). Gideon objects that his clan, his 'elef, is the weakest and he the least; God replies "I will be with you" (6:16), and Gideon asks for a sign (6:17). Saul (1 Samuel 9:21) and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:6–8) give the same kind of answer. Scholars call this the "call narrative" form. In each case the weakness of the one called shows that the power is God's (1 Corinthians 1:26–29).

a: flat bread made from an ephah of flour
t: A lavish meal in a famine
p: An ephah was a large measure, perhaps half a bushel. In hard times this was a costly gift.
b: An ephah of flour, very roughly twenty to forty pounds, would make a great deal of bread. Bread without yeast (matsot) was quick to bake, which suits a guest who is waiting (Genesis 18:6; Genesis 19:3). Gideon cooks a young goat, a meal for an honored guest, like Abraham's for his three visitors (Genesis 18:6–8). In the middle of Midian's raids, when Israel had "nothing to live on" (6:4), this was a large sacrifice. The word for his "gift" (minchah) also means an offering, and the meal becomes one.

a: Fire went up from the rock and ate up the meat and the flat bread
p: Fire from God accepting an offering appears at the tabernacle, with Manoah, and on Mount Carmel.
b: Fire from the LORD consumed the first offerings on the new altar (Leviticus 9:24), and the angel of the LORD rises in the flame of Manoah's offering (13:19–20). Elijah's sacrifice is burned by fire from heaven (1 Kings 18:38), and so is David's (1 Chronicles 21:26). Here the fire comes up out of the rock itself at the touch of a staff. The sign Gideon asked for (6:17) is given: the guest is not a man. The angel's staff recalls Moses' staff, which brought water from the rock (Exodus 17:6).

a: Now I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face!
p: Gideon fears death for seeing God's messenger. The Bible says no one can see God and live, yet some did.
b: God told Moses, "no human being can see me and stay alive" (Exodus 33:20). Yet Jacob said, "I have seen God face to face, and still my life was rescued" (Genesis 32:30), and Manoah fears death for the same reason as Gideon (13:22). The LORD's answer, "Peace to you. Do not be afraid. You will not die," turns fear into a name for the altar (6:24). Jewish and Christian readers have explained the tension by distinguishing God's full glory, which no one can see, from forms in which he chooses to appear (John 1:18).

a: The LORD Is Peace
p: YHWH Shalom, in the KJV "Jehovah-shalom," names the altar for the LORD's word "Peace to you."
b: Gideon names the altar YHWH Shalom. Shalom means peace, wholeness and well-being, and here first of all safety: Gideon will not die. Other places named with God's name include "The LORD Will See" (Genesis 22:14), "The LORD Is My Flag" (Exodus 17:15) and "The LORD Is There" (Ezekiel 48:35). The KJV's "Jehovah-shalom" comes from reading the vowels of Adonai with the letters YHWH, a form found in the Middle Ages. Ironically, this altar to the LORD stands in the same town where Gideon will later set up his ephod (8:27).

a: the second bull, seven years old
p: The Hebrew speaks of a young bull and a "second bull" seven years old. Whether there are one or two bulls is unclear.
b: The Hebrew reads "the young bull of the ox that belongs to your father, and the second bull, seven years." Some readers count two bulls, one perhaps to pull down the altar and one to sacrifice; others take the "and" as "that is," one bull, the second-born of the herd. A seven-year-old bull is unusually old for a sacrifice, and many scholars think the age is meant to match Midian's seven years (6:1): the bull raised in the years of oppression is offered to end it. Some think the bull had been kept for Baal.
orig: פַּר־הַשּׁוֹר ... וּפַר הַשֵּׁנִי שֶׁבַע שָׁנִים (par-hashor ... ufar hasheni sheva' shanim)

a: chop down the Asherah pole that stands beside it
p: Gideon's first task is to carry out the old command: pull down the altars and chop down the Asherah poles.
b: Deuteronomy commanded: "pull down their altars, break their standing stones to pieces, chop down their Asherah poles and burn their carved images" (Deuteronomy 7:5), and forbade planting "any kind of tree as an Asherah pole beside the altar of the LORD" (Deuteronomy 16:21). Gideon must clean his own family's shrine before he can fight Midian. Many readers see the order as the point: the enemy outside is a result of the idol inside. The new altar is built on "this stronghold," perhaps the hilltop refuge where the clan sheltered, and the old Asherah becomes firewood for the LORD's offering.

a: If he is a god, let him take up his own case
p: Joash's challenge sounds like Elijah's later mockery on Mount Carmel.
b: Joash, the owner of the Baal altar, turns the crowd's anger back on them: a god who needs people to defend him is no god. He even threatens death for anyone who "takes up his case," the very penalty they want for Gideon. Elijah later mocks the prophets of Baal in the same spirit: perhaps their god is asleep or away (1 Kings 18:27). Isaiah makes the same argument against idols that cannot speak or save (Isaiah 44:9–20). Why Joash changed sides the text does not say. Perhaps his son's courage moved him, or perhaps he was protecting his family.

a: So that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal
p: The text explains Jerubbaal as "Let Baal contend." The name may once have meant "Baal contends" or "Baal is great."
b: Yerubba'al is explained from riv, "contend, argue a case," as a mocking name: let Baal fight him if he can. Many scholars think it was first an ordinary name honoring Baal, "Baal contends [for him]" or "may Baal be great," common at a time when ba'al, "lord," was also used of Israel's God. Later writers disliked the Baal element and changed it: 2 Samuel 11:21 calls him Jerubbesheth, putting boshet, "shame," in place of Baal. Judges uses both names for him, Gideon and Jerubbaal, sometimes in the same verse (7:1; 8:35).

a: the Spirit of the LORD put Gideon on like clothing
p: The Hebrew says the Spirit "clothed itself with" Gideon: the Spirit puts the man on like a garment.
b: Ruach YHWH lavshah et-Gid'on means the Spirit "put on" Gideon. Most translations say "came upon," which hides the picture of God's Spirit wearing a man like clothing and moving in him. The same phrase is used of Amasai (1 Chronicles 12:18) and Zechariah the priest (2 Chronicles 24:20). Elsewhere people "put on" righteousness or strength (Job 29:14; Isaiah 51:9), and Paul tells believers to "put on" Christ (Romans 13:14). Gideon, who hid in a winepress, now calls out his clan with a ram's horn.
orig: וְרוּחַ יְהוָה לָבְשָׁה אֶת־גִּדְעוֹן (veruach YHWH lavshah et-Gid'on)

a: I am putting a wool fleece out here on the threshing floor
p: Gideon has God's promise and a sign already, yet asks for two more. Readers have praised and blamed him for it.
b: Gideon had a direct promise (6:14–16) and a sign of fire (6:21). Asking again looks like doubt, and the law said, "Do not put the LORD your God to the test" (Deuteronomy 6:16); Gideon himself fears God's anger (6:39). Yet God answers him twice, patiently. Many teachers warn against "putting out a fleece" to make decisions, since Gideon was seeking courage to obey a known command, not guidance. Others see God meeting weak faith with kindness. The first test was not very hard, since a fleece holds dew; the second, a dry fleece on wet ground, was the real wonder. On the Christian reading of the fleece as a symbol, see 6:40.

a: the fleece alone stayed dry, and on all the ground there was dew
p: Church fathers read the fleece as Israel and the ground as the nations, or as Mary receiving the Word.
b: Origen in his homilies on Judges read the first sign, dew on the fleece alone, as God's grace given first to Israel, and the second, dew on all the ground but not the fleece, as grace spread to the nations. Other Christian writers, such as Ambrose, joined the fleece to Psalm 72:6, where the Greek reads that the king will come down "like rain on a fleece," and saw it as a picture of the Word coming quietly into Mary's womb. Jewish readers did not read it this way and took the fleece as a sign for Gideon alone. The dew itself was a sign of God's blessing (Genesis 27:28; Hosea 14:5).

a: the spring of Harod
p: Harod sounds like the word for "trembling." Two verses later the trembling men are sent home.
b: The spring of Harod ('En Charod) is usually identified with a large spring at the foot of Mount Gilboa, on the south side of the Jezreel Valley, facing the hill of Moreh across the plain where Midian camped. Its name sounds like chared, "trembling," the word used in 7:3: "Whoever is scared and shaking (chared), let him turn back." The pun is lost in English. Saul later camped by a spring in Jezreel before his last battle on Gilboa (1 Samuel 29:1), a darker story at the same place.

a: Israel might glorify itself at my expense and say, 'My own hand rescued me.'
p: God cuts the army so that no one can take the credit. The theme runs from Deuteronomy to Paul.
b: Deuteronomy warned Israel against saying, "My own strength and the power of my hand have won me this wealth" (Deuteronomy 8:17). Here the danger is the same in war. God reduces Gideon's force from 32,000 to 300 so that the victory can only be his. Jonathan says, "The LORD is not held back. He can save with many or with few" (1 Samuel 14:6), and Zechariah, "not by strength and not by force, but by my Spirit" (Zechariah 4:6). Paul applies the idea to the church: God chose the weak so that no one may boast before him (1 Corinthians 1:27–29).
r: Deuteronomy 8:17–18; 1 Samuel 14:6; Zechariah 4:6; Psalm 20:7; Psalm 44:3; 1 Corinthians 1:27–29; 2 Corinthians 12:9

a: Whoever is scared and shaking, let him turn back and be off from Mount Gilead.
p: Gideon applies the war law of Deuteronomy 20:8: the fearful go home. But why "Mount Gilead"?
b: Deuteronomy's rules for war say: "Is anyone afraid and fainthearted? Let him go back home, so that his brothers' hearts do not melt like his" (Deuteronomy 20:8). Gideon, himself a fearful man, announces this, and two-thirds of the army leave. "Mount Gilead" is a puzzle, since Gilead lies east of the Jordan and the camp is west of it, at Harod. Some scholars read "Gilboa," the mountain above the spring; others take the verb yitspor as "turn round" or "slip away" and the place as an unknown local hill. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew name.

a: Put everyone who laps up the water with his tongue, the way a dog laps, in one group
p: Were the lappers the alert soldiers, or the worst ones? Readers since Josephus have disagreed.
b: Many readers think the lappers were chosen because they stayed alert, scooping water to their mouths while watching for the enemy. Josephus read it the other way: those who drank in a hurry were the fearful, and God picked the cowards so that the victory would be clearly his. Most modern scholars think the test is not about character at all; it is simply a way to sort the men, and God took the smaller group. The text is also unclear about who put their hands to their mouths: as it stands, the three hundred lapped "from their hands" (7:6), yet 7:5 compares them to dogs lapping with the tongue. Many scholars think the phrase about hands once belonged with the kneelers.

a: They took the people's food and their rams' horns in hand.
p: The Hebrew is unclear about who took what, but it seems the three hundred ended up with the others' horns.
b: The Hebrew says "they took the provisions of the people in their hand, and their rams' horns," without saying who "they" are; the Plain English leaves it open, though most readers take it as the three hundred. With a change of letters, "provisions of the people" becomes "jars of the people" (kaddei for tsedat), which would supply the jars used in 7:16. Either way, the three hundred ended up with enough horns for every man to have one, which explains the plan: normally a few horn-blowers led a large force, so three hundred horns would sound like a huge army. The rest of the army was sent away, "each to his tent," an old phrase for going home.
orig: וַיִּקְחוּ אֶת־צֵדָה הָעָם בְּיָדָם וְאֵת שׁוֹפְרֹתֵיהֶם (vayyiqchu et-tsedah ha'am beyadam ve'et shoferotehem)

a: like a swarm of locusts
p: Judith pictures the Assyrian army with this verse's two images: locusts, and sand past counting.
b: Huge armies are often compared to locusts or to sand (6:5; Joshua 11:4; 1 Samuel 13:5). Judith, a book Catholic and Orthodox Christians include in the Old Testament, joins the two images as this verse does. When the Assyrian army marches west, the book says: "A large mixed crowd went out with them, like locusts, like the sand of the earth, for there was no counting how many they were" (Judith 2:20). The echo points to the same lesson as Gideon's story. God cut Gideon's army to three hundred men so that Israel could not boast (7:2). In Judith a whole army falls to one widow.

a: A round loaf of barley bread was rolling over and over into Midian's camp.
t: The barley loaf and the tent
p: Barley bread was poor farmers' food. The loaf stands for Israel the farmer; the tent for Midian the nomad.
b: Barley was cheaper than wheat and was the bread of the poor (Ruth 2:17; John 6:9). A round loaf (tselil, an uncertain word) rolling into the camp and knocking over "the tent" pictures the farming people of Israel overturning the tent-dwelling raiders. The interpretation comes from an enemy soldier, which makes it a sign to Gideon: even Midian knows his name and fears it. God had told Gideon that by listening his hands would "be strong" (7:11). Dreams as messages from God appear across the Bible, often interpreted by outsiders or for them (Genesis 40–41; Daniel 2).

a: Gideon bowed down in worship
p: For the first time Gideon worships without asking for another sign.
b: The verb hishtachavah means to bow down low, and before God it means worship. After the fire from the rock, two fleece tests and now the dream, Gideon at last responds with worship and command rather than doubt. His words to the army repeat God's own promise of 7:9: the LORD has put Midian's camp in their power. Many readers see this verse as the high point of Gideon's faith.

a: at the start of the middle watch
p: The night was split into three watches. The middle watch began around ten at night, just after the guards changed.
b: In Israel's reckoning the night had three watches (Lamentations 2:19; Exodus 14:24, "the morning watch"); later, under Roman rule, there were four (Mark 6:48). Attacking at the start of the middle watch meant striking when the new guards had just settled and most of the camp was asleep. Breaking the jars made a sudden crash and revealed torches all around, while three hundred horns blew. In the dark, the raiders could not tell friend from foe. Ancient writers on strategy record similar night tricks, but this one also has the marks of a holy war, where God causes the panic (7:22).

a: A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!
p: The battle cry puts Gideon's name beside the LORD's. Some readers see the start of his pride.
b: Gideon told his men to shout "For the LORD and for Gideon!" (7:18). They add "a sword," the word the Midianite used in interpreting the dream ("the sword of Gideon," 7:14). No sword is actually used by the three hundred; the LORD sets the enemy's swords against each other (7:22). Many literary readers, such as Webb and Block, see a quiet warning in Gideon's name standing next to God's, given what follows: punishing his own towns, taking gold, and making an ephod (chapter 8). Others think the cry simply names God's chosen leader, as Moses was named with God (Exodus 14:31).

a: the LORD turned each man's sword against his comrade all through the camp
p: In several holy-war stories, God throws the enemy into such confusion that they kill each other.
b: The same thing happens to the Philistines in Saul's day (1 Samuel 14:20), and to Ammon, Moab and Edom in the time of Jehoshaphat, when Judah only sang and watched (2 Chronicles 20:22–23). Ezekiel pictures God's final defeat of Gog this way (Ezekiel 38:21), and Haggai speaks of horses and riders falling "each by the sword of his brother" (Haggai 2:22). In these stories God's people barely fight. Places in this verse are uncertain, but the flight ran east and southeast toward the Jordan.

a: take control of the waters ahead of them as far as Beth-barah, and of the Jordan
p: Gideon calls in Ephraim to cut off the retreat at the river crossings, as Ehud did.
b: The fleeing army had to cross the Jordan or its side streams to reach the desert. Ephraim, the strongest tribe in the central hills, was asked to hold the crossings, as Ehud's men had done against Moab (3:28). This is the first time Ephraim appears in the story, and its pride at being called late leads to the quarrel of 8:1–3. Beth-barah is unknown; it may mean "house of the ford." The pattern of Ephraim's anger returns with Jephthah (12:1), with a bloodier end.

a: Oreb and Zeeb
p: The two commanders' names mean "Raven" and "Wolf." Their deaths named two places and were long remembered.
b: 'Orev is "raven" and Ze'ev is "wolf," names of desert creatures, perhaps nicknames or clan symbols. The places where they died were named the Rock of Oreb and the Winepress of Zeeb. Isaiah remembers "the beating he gave Midian at Oreb's Rock" (Isaiah 10:26), and Psalm 83:11 prays that God will treat Israel's enemies like Oreb and like Zeeb. There is irony in Zeeb dying at a winepress, the place where Gideon hid. Cutting off enemies' heads and bringing them to the leader was a common practice, as David did with Goliath's (1 Samuel 17:54).

a: not calling us when you went to fight Midian
p: Ephraim complains twice in Judges of being left out. Gideon calms them; Jephthah fights them.
b: Ephraim was the leading tribe of the north, Joshua's tribe, with the sanctuary at Shiloh in its land. Its complaint is about honor and plunder, not the danger it missed. Gideon answers with flattery and humility, and their anger cools; Proverbs says, "A soft-spoken answer turns fury back" (Proverbs 15:1). When Ephraim makes the same complaint to Jephthah, he answers with accusation, and forty-two thousand die (12:1–6). Literary readers see the two scenes as a measure of decline: tribal jealousy that Gideon could still defuse has, a generation later, become civil war.

a: Isn't what Ephraim picks up after the harvest better than Abiezer's whole grape harvest?
p: Gideon's proverb: Ephraim's leftovers outweigh his clan's whole crop. Capturing two princes beats his own victory.
b: 'Olelot are the grapes left on the vines after the harvest for the poor to glean (Leviticus 19:10; Deuteronomy 24:21), and batsir is the main grape harvest. Gideon says Ephraim's small share of the battle, the capture of Oreb and Zeeb, was worth more than his whole clan's work. It is a clever, humble answer, and it works. The picture of grape harvest also fits the story: Gideon threshed in a winepress, and Zeeb died at one (6:11; 7:25).
orig: עֹלְלוֹת אֶפְרַיִם ... מִבְצִיר אֲבִיעֶזֶר ('olelot Efrayim ... mibbetsir Avi'ezer)

a: He said to the men of Succoth
p: Both towns were east of the Jordan, near the Jabbok River where Jacob had wrestled.
b: Succoth, "booths," was where Jacob built shelters for his cattle (Genesis 33:17); it is often placed at Tell Deir Alla, in the Jordan Valley near the Jabbok, the site where an inscription about Balaam son of Beor was found. Penuel, "face of God," was where Jacob wrestled and said, "I have seen God face to face" (Genesis 32:30). Succoth was given to Gad (Joshua 13:27). Their leaders refuse to feed Gideon's men, probably fearing Midian's revenge if Gideon failed. The refusal of hospitality to fellow Israelites is a theme that grows darker in the book's last chapters (19:15).

a: Is the hand of Zebah and Zalmunna in your hand right now
p: The officials' taunt may refer to the custom of cutting off enemies' hands to count the dead.
b: The Hebrew says "Is the palm of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand?" Egyptian reliefs, such as those of Ramesses III at Medinet Habu, show scribes counting piles of severed hands after battle, a way to tally the enemy dead and reward the soldiers. The officials mean: you have not won yet, so why should we risk helping you? Zebah and Zalmunna are probably mocking forms of the kings' names: Zevach sounds like "sacrifice" and Tsalmunna' like "protection refused."
orig: הֲכַף זֶבַח וְצַלְמֻנָּע עַתָּה בְּיָדֶךָ (hakhaf Zevach veTsalmunna' 'attah beyadekha)

a: I will thresh your bodies with thorns from the wilderness and with briers
p: Gideon threatens to "thresh" the leaders. It may mean flogging with thorns, or dragging threshing sledges over them.
b: The verb dush means to thresh, as with grain. Gideon, who threshed his wheat in hiding (6:11), now threatens to thresh men. It may mean beating them with thorny branches, or laying them on thorns and dragging threshing sledges over them, a punishment Amos condemns when Damascus did it to Gilead (Amos 1:3). Some think it was a way of tearing the skin. Gideon carries it out in 8:16, where the Greek reads "threshed" (see the variant). The punishment of fellow Israelites is the first sign of Gideon's harder side.

a: a hundred and twenty thousand sword-bearing men had fallen
p: The numbers are huge for desert raiders. Readers take them as literal, rounded, or counts of units.
b: A hundred and twenty thousand dead and fifteen thousand left would make an army of 135,000 camel riders, far more than the desert could support by most historians' estimates. As with other large numbers in the Old Testament, some read 'elef as a clan unit (see 1:4), giving 120 units; others take the figures as rounded or as expressions of an overwhelming host, like "as many as the grains of sand" (7:12). Traditional readers often accept the numbers as given, noting that the coalition included Amalek and the peoples of the East.

a: the youth listed in writing for him the officials of Succoth and its elders
t: A young man who could write
p: A passing youth can write a list of seventy-seven names. Writing was spreading in this period.
b: The verse assumes that an ordinary young man could write, or at least that someone in a small town could. By the early Iron Age the alphabet was in use in Canaan, and short inscriptions have been found, such as the abecedary (an alphabet practice text) from Izbet Sartah, a village near Aphek dated to about 1200 to 1000 BC. Scholars debate how widespread literacy was; some think scribes were few. The list gave Gideon exact names: his punishment would fall on the leaders, seventy-seven men, not on the whole town.

a: What about the men you killed at Tabor?
p: The story suddenly reveals that Gideon's own brothers were killed. His pursuit becomes a blood feud.
b: Nothing earlier mentions the killing of Gideon's brothers at Tabor. Now the long chase across the Jordan looks partly personal: Gideon acts as the "avenger of blood" (go'el haddam, Numbers 35:19) for his mother's sons. The kings' answer, "Each one looked like a king's son," is flattery, and perhaps a hint of Gideon's royal bearing. Many readers see the war turning here from the LORD's war into Gideon's, with his oath "As the LORD lives" used to justify his own vengeance. Others see a legitimate execution of murderers.

a: But the youth would not draw his sword
p: Gideon's son is afraid, just as Gideon once was. Killing a king was an honor, and a shame for the king to die by a boy.
b: Asking a son to kill a captured king was a way of giving him honor and of shaming the enemy, who would die at a boy's hand. Jether is afraid, "because he was still young," and the echo of his father's fear (6:15, 27; 7:10) is hard to miss. The kings ask Gideon to do it himself, since "a man's strength matches the man," a proverb meaning a real man should strike. The scene prepares for the next generation: of Gideon's seventy sons, the one who takes power will be Abimelech, who has no such fear (9:5).

a: the moon-shaped ornaments
p: Saharonim were crescent-shaped pendants, likely tied to the worship of the moon god.
b: The saharonim were small crescent moons, worn by people (Isaiah 3:18) and hung on camels' necks. The moon god, Sin in Mesopotamia and Yarikh in Canaan, was widely worshiped by desert peoples, and such charms were thought to protect. Gideon takes them as trophies. Their mention again in 8:26 among the gold used for the ephod hints that pagan ornaments went into Israel's new object of worship.

a: The LORD will rule over you.
p: Gideon says no to a dynasty. Readers debate whether he meant it, and whether Judges is for or against kings.
b: The men of Israel offer Gideon what amounts to kingship, a rule passed to his son and grandson. He refuses with a clear statement that the LORD is Israel's ruler, an idea taken up in Samuel's warning (1 Samuel 8:7; 1 Samuel 12:12). Martin Buber read the line as the heart of an early Israelite rejection of human kings. But Gideon then takes gold, makes an ephod, has many wives and names a son Abimelech, "my father is king" (8:24–31). Many scholars therefore read his words as polite refusal masking royal behavior. The book as a whole holds two views in tension: kings are a rejection of God (8:23; 9:7–15), yet without a king "everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (17:6; 21:25).

a: because they were Ishmaelites
p: The text calls the Midianites Ishmaelites, as Genesis 37 does. The name could mean caravan traders in general.
b: In Joseph's story the traders who bought him are called both Ishmaelites and Midianites (Genesis 37:25–28, 36). Here, too, the Midianites wore gold "because they were Ishmaelites." Many scholars think "Ishmaelite" was used for desert traders and nomads in general, who were known for wearing gold, rather than for a separate people. Others think the two groups were related through Abraham's sons by Hagar and Keturah (Genesis 25:1–2, 12–16).

a: seventeen hundred shekels of gold
p: About forty-three pounds of gold, a king's wealth, from earrings alone.
b: A shekel weighed about 11.4 grams, so 1,700 shekels came to roughly 19 kilograms, or about 43 pounds of gold. Added to it were the crescents, pendants, purple royal robes and camel chains. Purple dye, made from sea snails, was the most costly dye in the ancient world and a mark of kings. The amount echoes the gold earrings Aaron collected for the golden calf (Exodus 32:2–4) and anticipates Deuteronomy's warning that a king must not pile up gold (Deuteronomy 17:17).

a: Gideon made it into an ephod
p: An ephod was a priest's vest, sometimes used to ask God for answers. Gideon's seems to have become an idol.
b: In Exodus the ephod is the high priest's richly worked vest, holding the breastpiece with the Urim and Thummim (Exodus 28:6–30). In Samuel, priests "bring the ephod" to ask God's will (1 Samuel 23:9; 1 Samuel 30:7), and Goliath's sword is kept behind one (1 Samuel 21:9). Micah later makes "an ephod and household gods" for his shrine (17:5). With forty-three pounds of gold, Gideon's ephod may have been an image or a gold-covered object for seeking oracles. Gideon, the man who asked for signs, may have wanted a permanent way to ask God. The result was worship of the object itself.

a: All Israel went after it there like a prostitute
p: Gold earrings from the people, an object of worship, and Israel led astray: the story echoes Aaron's calf.
b: At Sinai Aaron told the people to "pull off the gold rings in the ears of your wives, your sons and your daughters," and made a calf (Exodus 32:2–4). Gideon asks for gold earrings and makes an ephod, and "all Israel" goes astray with it. Later Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Dan and Bethel (1 Kings 12:28–30). The verse uses the word "trap" (moqesh) from 2:3: what the angel said the Canaanites' gods would be, Gideon's own gift to God became. The man who tore down Baal's altar ended by setting up a new object of false worship in the same town.

a: because he had many wives
p: Seventy sons and many wives were signs of a king, which Gideon had just refused to be.
b: Seventy sons implies a large harem, like those of kings. Deuteronomy warns that a king "must not take many wives for himself, or his heart will turn aside" (Deuteronomy 17:17). The number seventy appears again in Abimelech's massacre (9:5), in Abdon's seventy grandsons and riders (12:14), and in Ahab's seventy sons, killed by Jehu (2 Kings 10:1–7). Gideon lives like a king without the title. Polygamy is reported, not commanded, in the Old Testament, and its stories usually show its costs.

a: he gave him the name Abimelech
p: Abimelech means "my father is king." The name says what Gideon denied.
b: Avimelekh means "my father is king" or "the king is my father," where "king" could refer to God. The phrase here is unusual: literally "he set his name Abimelech," which some scholars take to mean Gideon renamed him or gave him a special title. Coming right after "I will not rule over you" (8:23), the name reads as a sign of Gideon's real ambitions, or at least of what his son would hear in it. The son of a concubine from Shechem, a Canaanite town, he will make himself king there (9:1–6).

a: They made Baal-berith their god.
p: Baal-berith means "lord of the covenant." Israel swaps its covenant with the LORD for a covenant Baal.
b: Ba'al Berit was the god of Shechem's temple (9:4). In 9:46 the same temple is called that of El-berit, "God of the covenant." Shechem was the place of Joshua's covenant with the LORD (Joshua 24:25), so the name is bitterly ironic: the town of Israel's covenant now worships a Baal of covenant. Some scholars think the local god guarded treaties between Shechem and its neighbors, perhaps including Israelite clans. Others think Israelites had blended their covenant God with Baal. Either way, the cycle has fully returned to 2:11–13.

a: Nor did they show loyal love to the family of Jerubbaal
p: Hesed, loyal love, was owed to Gideon's family for what he did. Its absence opens chapter 9.
b: Hesed is the faithful kindness owed within a relationship, here the gratitude owed to a rescuer's family. Jotham's speech will turn on this very point: whether Shechem acted "in good faith and integrity" toward Jerubbaal's house (9:16, 19). The verse sets two failures side by side: Israel forgot the LORD who rescued them (8:34) and the man through whom he did it. The book's first act of hesed was promised to a Canaanite at Bethel (1:24); here Israel will not show it even to its own.

a: Abimelech son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem
t: Shechem, a Canaanite city in Israel
p: Shechem was an old Canaanite city at the center of the hills. Its kings had a history of using hired men to grab power.
b: Shechem (Tell Balata, near modern Nablus) lay in the pass between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim. It appears in the Amarna letters of the fourteenth century BC, where its ruler Labayu and later his sons are accused by neighbors of building power with hired bands of outlaws (habiru). Abimelech's story fits that pattern closely. In the Bible Shechem is the place of Abraham's altar (Genesis 12:6–7), Jacob's purchase and Dinah's rape (Genesis 33:18–34:31), and Joshua's covenant (Joshua 24). Here it seems to be a mixed town of Canaanites and Israelites, still loyal to "Hamor, Shechem's father" (9:28).

a: the lords of Shechem
p: Ba'ale Shekhem means the town's owners or leading citizens. The word ba'al echoes the town's god.
b: Ba'ale Shekhem, "the baals of Shechem," means its landowners or citizens with full rights, the men who decided the town's affairs. Ba'ale, "lords," appears sixteen times in chapter 9, thirteen of them in the phrase "lords of Shechem." Since ba'al means "owner, lord," and the town's god was Baal-berith (8:33; 9:4), the repetition is pointed: the lords of Shechem serve the Lord of the covenant, and both will be destroyed. The Plain English uses "lords" to keep the link; a gloss gives the plainer sense.

a: Remember, I am your own bone and flesh.
p: An appeal to kinship. The same words win David the kingship of Israel.
b: "Bone and flesh" means close family, as when Laban says to Jacob, "You really are my bone and my flesh" (Genesis 29:14), or the man says of the woman, "bone from my bones / and flesh from my flesh" (Genesis 2:23). The tribes use the same words to make David king (2 Samuel 5:1), and David to win back Judah (2 Samuel 19:12–13). Abimelech's mother was from Shechem (8:31), so he appeals to the town's blood ties against his father's seventy Israelite sons. Kinship politics will be the theme of the whole chapter: "He's our brother" (9:3).

a: seventy pieces of silver from the temple of Baal-berith
p: The temple treasury funds a coup: one piece of silver for each brother to be killed.
b: Temples in the ancient Near East held treasure and often acted as banks for their towns; kings drew on them in emergencies (1 Kings 15:18). The seventy pieces of silver, one per son of Jerubbaal, buy Abimelech a band of hired killers. The price of a slave was thirty shekels (Exodus 21:32), so seventy pieces was a modest sum for a band of hired men, about two slaves' price. That a god's money pays for the murder of the sons of the man who tore down Baal's altar is the story's grim joke.

a: empty, reckless men
p: Anashim reqim, "empty men," were landless drifters who hired out as fighters. Jephthah and David gathered such men too.
b: Reqim means "empty": men with no land, no family standing and nothing to lose, the kind who gathered around warlords. Pochazim means "reckless" or "undisciplined" (Genesis 49:4, of Reuben). Jephthah's band in Tob is made of the same "empty men" (11:3), and David's early followers in the cave of Adullam were men in debt and distress (1 Samuel 22:2). Gregory Mobley has studied these bands as part of Israel's heroic tradition. Abimelech is the first to use them against his own family.

a: killed his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on a single stone
p: Killing them on one stone looks like a mass execution, or even a sacrifice. Only the youngest escapes.
b: "One stone" suggests the brothers were killed one by one at a single place, like animals slaughtered on a stone (1 Samuel 14:33–34). The story's end turns on another stone: a millstone dropped by a woman (9:53). Jotham names the stone twice in his curse (9:18). Similar mass killings of a royal house come later: Jehu has Ahab's seventy sons killed (2 Kings 10:6–7), and Athaliah tries to wipe out David's line, but the youngest, Joash, is hidden and survives (2 Kings 11:1–3). Readers see the pattern: a usurper kills his brothers, one escapes, and justice follows.

a: Beth-millo
p: Millo means "fill," probably an earth-filled platform or fortress. Beth-millo may be the Tower of Shechem.
b: Millo' comes from the verb "to fill." In Jerusalem, "the Millo" was a built-up terrace or fortification (2 Samuel 5:9; 1 Kings 9:15). At Shechem, Beth-millo may be the citadel built on a filled platform, where the town's rulers or garrison lived. Many scholars think it is the same as "the Tower of Shechem" (9:46–49), which was destroyed by fire. The phrase "the lords of Shechem and Beth-millo" (9:20) then means the town and its fortress.

a: by the oak of the pillar at Shechem
t: The tree and the stone at Shechem
p: Shechem had an ancient sacred tree and standing stone, linked with Abraham, Jacob and Joshua.
b: Abraham's first altar in the land was at "the great tree of Moreh" at Shechem (Genesis 12:6). Jacob buried his household's foreign gods "under the oak that is by Shechem" (Genesis 35:4). Joshua set up "a large stone ... under the oak that was by the sanctuary of the LORD" as a witness to the covenant (Joshua 24:26). The "oak of the pillar" (elon mutsav) is probably that same place. Abimelech is crowned at the very spot where Israel swore to serve the LORD alone. Excavators at Tell Balata found a large standing stone near the temple area.

a: he went and stood on top of Mount Gerizim
p: Mount Gerizim towers over Shechem. It was the mountain of blessing; Jotham speaks a curse from it.
b: Mount Gerizim rises about 2,800 feet above sea level, on the south side of the pass where Shechem lay. Moses had appointed it as the mountain from which the blessings of the covenant were to be spoken, with Ebal for the curses (Deuteronomy 11:29; Deuteronomy 27:12–13). The valley between them is narrow, and voices carry. Jotham uses the mountain of blessing to deliver a fable that ends in a curse (9:20, 57). The Samaritans later built their temple on Gerizim (John 4:20).

a: The trees went out once to anoint a king over themselves.
p: Jotham tells a fable, the oldest in the Bible. Talking plants were a known form in the ancient Near East.
b: A fable is a short story in which animals or plants speak, with a moral. The Bible has only two: this one and Jehoash's fable of the thistle and the cedar (2 Kings 14:9). Ancient Mesopotamia had "debate" poems in which trees and plants argue over which is most useful, such as "The Tamarisk and the Date Palm," known from texts of the second millennium BC. Jotham's fable is different: no tree wants to rule, because the useful ones are busy being useful. The genre is real and widespread; the specific story is Israel's own.

a: which brings honor to gods and humans
p: Olive oil was used to anoint kings and priests and in offerings. The fable speaks of "gods" in the plural.
b: Olive oil anointed kings and priests (1 Samuel 10:1; Exodus 29:7), went into grain offerings (Leviticus 2:1), and lit the sanctuary lamps. The word elohim can mean "God" or "gods." In the mouth of a tree speaking to Canaanite Shechem, many translators take it as "gods," since the vine's wine also "cheers" them (9:13). The Targum, uneasy with the idea of wine cheering God, paraphrased it. Psalm 104:15 praises God for "wine that cheers a person's heart, oil to make the face shine."

a: come, shelter in my shade
p: A thornbush gives no shade and burns easily. Its offer of protection is a joke and a threat.
b: The atad is a thorny shrub, perhaps the buckthorn, low to the ground. Its invitation to the tall cedars to "shelter in my shade" is absurd: kings were often called the shade of their people (Lamentations 4:20; Isaiah 30:2), but a bramble's shade is nothing. Dry thornbushes catch fire quickly and set fields ablaze (Exodus 22:6), and that is the real threat: if you are not loyal, my fire will burn even the cedars of Lebanon, the greatest trees. The fable's point is not subtle: Abimelech is a thornbush king.

a: did you act in good faith and integrity when you made Abimelech king?
t: Against kings, or against this king?
p: Is the fable against all kingship, or only against Abimelech and those who chose him? Readers differ.
b: Martin Buber called Jotham's fable the strongest anti-monarchic poem in world literature: the worthy trees refuse to rule, and only the worthless one accepts. Many scholars agree that it reflects an early Israelite suspicion of kings, shared with Gideon (8:23) and Samuel (1 Samuel 8). Others point out that Jotham's application (9:16–20) is about Shechem's ingratitude and Abimelech's crimes, not kingship in general, and that the book later laments having no king (17:6; 21:25). Traditional readers often take a middle view: the problem is a king chosen by people for selfish reasons rather than one chosen by God.

a: the son of his slave woman
p: Jotham calls Abimelech's mother a slave woman, though 8:31 calls her a concubine. It is meant as an insult.
b: In 8:31 Abimelech's mother is a pilegesh, a secondary wife. Jotham calls her an amah, a female slave. It is a slur, setting the Shechemite's son below Gideon's other children, but it may also reflect her real status. The same tension between the sons of a wife and the son of a lesser woman drives Jephthah's story (11:1–2) and goes back to Sarah and Hagar (Genesis 21:10). Jotham uses it to shame the lords of Shechem: they made a slave's son their king because "he is your brother."

a: Abimelech held power over Israel for three years.
t: Not called king by the narrator
p: The people "made him king," but the narrator says only that he "held power" (sarar), avoiding the word for reigning.
b: The lords of Shechem made Abimelech "king" (vayyamlikhu, 9:6), and Jotham's fable uses the word for reigning. But the narrator uses vayyasar, from sarar, "to act as prince, to rule," a word for an official rather than a king. "Over Israel" may be an exaggeration from Shechem's point of view; his power reached only a few towns in the hills. Three years is short, and the narrator does not dignify it as a reign.

a: God sent a harmful spirit
p: God sends a "bad spirit" to break the alliance. The Bible says the same of Saul and of Ahab's prophets.
b: Ruach ra'ah can mean an evil spirit or a spirit of ill will, a mood of distrust. God sends it "between" Abimelech and Shechem, and the alliance built on murder falls apart. A "harmful spirit from the LORD" troubles Saul (1 Samuel 16:14), and in Micaiah's vision a lying spirit goes out from God's council to Ahab's prophets (1 Kings 22:19–23). The Bible states God's control over evil boldly, while holding people responsible for their own acts (9:24). Jewish and Christian theologians have explained such texts as God permitting or directing evil for judgment, without being its author.

a: Gaal son of Ebed
p: Gaal's name may mean "loathing" and his father's means "slave." A rival to Abimelech who taunts him for serving.
b: Ga'al may come from a root meaning "loathe" or be related to a word for "dung beetle" in other languages; 'Eved means "slave" or "servant." Whether these were real names or the narrator's mockery, they fit the scene: the son of Slave asks, "Why should we serve him?" (9:28), using the verb 'avad, and urges Shechem to serve the men of Hamor instead. The irony echoes Jotham's taunt that Abimelech was a slave woman's son (9:18). Gaal is the second strongman of the chapter, and he too is thrown out.

a: they made a feast of praise
p: The grape harvest was a time of feasting and praise. At Shechem it became a drunken rally against Abimelech.
b: The word hillulim means "praises" and is used for the festival of fruit in Leviticus 19:24. Grape harvests were times of dancing and song (Isaiah 16:10; 21:19–21 at Shiloh). Here the feast is held in "the house of their god," Baal-berith's temple, and turns into cursing Abimelech. The vine had refused to be king in Jotham's fable because its wine "cheers gods and humans" (9:13); now the wine fuels rebellion.

a: the men of Hamor, Shechem's father
p: Gaal appeals to Shechem's Canaanite founding family, the house of Hamor from Genesis 34.
b: In Genesis, Shechem son of Hamor raped Dinah, and her brothers destroyed the town (Genesis 34:2, 25–29). Jacob had bought land there "from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father" (Genesis 33:19), and Joseph was buried on it (Joshua 24:32). Gaal calls the town back to its old Canaanite ruling family against a half-Israelite king, Jerubbaal's son. The words show that Shechem's population was still largely Canaanite, and that ethnic loyalties ran deep.

a: He sent messengers to Abimelech in secret
p: The Hebrew betormah may mean "with deceit" or name a place, Tormah, perhaps Arumah (9:41).
b: Betormah is found only here. It can be read as "at Tormah," an unknown place, or as "in deceit," from tarmah, "treachery." Many scholars think it is a scribal slip for "at Arumah," Abimelech's base in 9:41. The Greek witnesses guessed "secretly" and "with gifts." The Plain English follows the most common reading, which fits Zebul's double game: he is Abimelech's officer inside a town that has turned against him.

a: the Navel of the Land
p: Tabbur ha'arets, "navel of the land," may be a hilltop near Shechem, seen as the center of the country.
b: Tabbur means "navel." Ezekiel uses the same word of Israel's people, who "live at the center of the earth" (Ezekiel 38:12). Many ancient peoples spoke of a sacred center of the world: the Greeks marked the "navel" (omphalos) at Delphi with a stone, and later Jewish tradition said Jerusalem, or the temple's foundation stone, was the navel of the world. Shechem sits at the geographic center of the central hills, between Ebal and Gerizim. Some scholars translate simply "the high ground," from the hilltop's shape.

a: the Diviners' Oak
p: A tree where fortune-tellers worked. The law forbade such diviners (Deuteronomy 18:10).
b: Elon me'onenim means "oak of the soothsayers." The me'onen was a kind of diviner forbidden in Israel: "There must not be found among you anyone ... who reads signs, looks for omens" (Deuteronomy 18:10, where the same root is used). Sacred trees were common places for oracles. This may be the same tree as the "oak of the pillar" (9:6) or Moreh, "teacher" (Genesis 12:6). At Shechem the old tree of Abraham and Joshua had become a fortune-tellers' tree.

a: tore the town down and sowed it with salt
p: Scattering salt on a destroyed town was a curse that it stay barren. Shechem was destroyed in the twelfth century BC.
b: Salt makes soil barren, and ancient treaties and inscriptions sometimes curse a defeated place with salt or weeds so that nothing will grow or be rebuilt (Deuteronomy 29:23; Jeremiah 17:6). It may have been a ritual act more than a large-scale spreading. Excavations at Tell Balata led by G. Ernest Wright found that Shechem was destroyed in the twelfth century BC and then lay largely empty for a long time, and many archaeologists link that destruction with Abimelech. Shechem was later rebuilt, and Rehoboam was crowned there (1 Kings 12:1, 25).

a: the stronghold of the temple of El-berith
p: Shechem had a massive fortress temple. The people hid in its inner chamber, and Abimelech burned it over them.
b: Excavators at Shechem uncovered a huge temple with walls about 17 feet thick. Archaeologists call this type a "fortress temple" or migdal temple, from the Hebrew word for tower. Many identify it with "the Tower of Shechem" and the temple of El-berith, but its date is disputed. The American excavation reports dated the massive building to the Middle Bronze Age, about 1650–1550 BC, too early for Abimelech. G. Ernest Wright linked El-berith to a rebuilt Late Bronze phase with thinner walls. Lawrence Stager re-dated the use of the great building into Iron Age I and so tied it to this chapter. The Iron I destruction of the city is on firmer ground. The tseriach was some inner or underground chamber, a refuge that became a furnace. El-berith, "God of the covenant," is the same god as Baal-berith (8:33; 9:4), or a title that once belonged to Israel's own God.
orig: צְרִיחַ בֵּית אֵל בְּרִית (tseriach bet El berit)

a: What you have seen me do, hurry and do just as I have done!
p: Abimelech gives his men the order his father Gideon gave at Midian's camp.
b: Gideon told his three hundred, "Keep your eyes on me and copy me ... whatever I do, you do too" (7:17). His son uses nearly the same command, but against an Israelite and Canaanite town of his own people. The father led a holy war against foreign raiders; the son leads a massacre of his own subjects. Literary readers see this as one of many echoes that show the decline from Gideon to Abimelech. Mount Zalmon, "dark mountain," is named again in Psalm 68:14.

a: a woman threw an upper millstone down on Abimelech's head
p: Women ground grain daily with a hand mill. The upper stone was heavy enough to kill. It was remembered for generations.
b: The pelach rekhev, "the rider piece," was the upper stone of a hand mill, a heavy loaf-shaped stone rubbed back and forth on a lower slab. Grinding was women's daily work (Exodus 11:5; Matthew 24:41). From the tower roof it became a weapon. Abimelech, who killed seventy brothers "on a single stone" (9:5), is killed by a single stone. Generations later Joab expected David to cite this very event as a warning against fighting too close to a wall (2 Samuel 11:21). The unnamed woman joins Jael as a woman who kills a tyrant.

a: so no one can say about me, 'A woman killed him.'
t: Saved from shame, but not in memory
p: Abimelech asks to be killed to avoid dying by a woman. It did not work: the story is remembered as a woman's deed.
b: Dying at a woman's hand was a disgrace for a warrior, as Deborah's word to Barak assumed (4:9). Abimelech's armor-bearer kills him, as Saul asks his own armor-bearer to do, to avoid shame at the hands of the uncircumcised (1 Samuel 31:4). But 2 Samuel 11:21 still says, "Wasn't it a woman who dropped an upper millstone on him from the wall?" The proud man's last request fails: history credits the woman.

a: So God paid back the evil Abimelech had done to his father
p: The chapter ends by naming God as the one who repaid both Abimelech and Shechem, fulfilling Jotham's curse.
b: Chapter 9 has no judge, no crying out, and no rescue. God appears only to send the spirit of discord (9:23) and, at the end, to repay. The punishment fits the crime closely: Abimelech and Shechem rose together and fell by each other, as Jotham's curse said (9:20); a stone for a stone. The book opened with Adoni-bezek saying "What I did to others, God has now done to me" (1:7). Many readers see the chapter as a story of providence: God works through the mixed motives of people to bring justice, without any miracle.

a: Tola son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar
p: Five judges get only a few lines each. Scholars call them the minor judges and debate where the lists came from.
b: Tola, Jair (10:1–5), Ibzan, Elon and Abdon (12:8–15) are described in a set pattern: name, home, years, sometimes family wealth, death and burial. There are no enemies or battles. Martin Noth thought they came from an old list of officials who "judged" all Israel in a legal sense, and that the editor borrowed the title for the war heroes. Others think the notes simply fill out the period and help make up twelve judges. Tola and Puah are both names of Issachar's clans (Genesis 46:13; Numbers 26:23), so these may be clan memories told as persons.

a: He had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty towns
p: A pun: 'ayarim means "donkeys" and, spelled the same here, "towns." Riding donkeys was a sign of rank.
b: The Hebrew writes both words as 'ayarim: thirty sons on thirty young donkeys ('ayarim) with thirty towns ('ayarim, an unusual form of 'arim). The wordplay marks Jair as a wealthy chief. Riding donkeys was what leaders did (5:10; Zechariah 9:9). Havvoth-jair, "the tent villages of Jair," are traced to Jair son of Manasseh in Moses' time (Numbers 32:41; Deuteronomy 3:14). Either the same name was reused for a later clan leader or two traditions about one area have merged.

a: the gods of Aram, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites and the gods of the Philistines
p: The list counts seven: Baals, Ashtoreths, and the gods of five nations. Israel's idolatry is now complete.
b: The Baals and the Ashtoreths, then the gods of Aram, Sidon, Moab, Ammon and Philistia: seven in all, the number of fullness. In 10:11–12 God lists seven nations from which he rescued Israel. The match is deliberate: seven rescues answered by seven sets of gods. Chemosh of Moab and Milcom of Ammon appear later (11:24; 1 Kings 11:5–7); Dagon of the Philistines appears in Samson's story (16:23). This is the fullest list of Israel's idols in the book and marks the low point before Jephthah.

a: they shattered and crushed the Israelites
p: Two verbs that sound alike, ra'ats and ratsats, stress the violence of the oppression.
b: Vayyir'atsu vayroetsetsu: the verbs ra'ats, "shatter," and ratsats, "crush," are used together for a crushing blow (Exodus 15:6 uses ra'ats of God shattering the enemy; Deuteronomy 28:33 uses ratsats of being "crushed all your days"). The sound play makes the line hard to forget. "That year" seems to mark the start of eighteen years of oppression east of the Jordan.

a: Maon
p: No oppression by Maon is told anywhere. The Greek reads Midian, which fits the story of Gideon.
b: The Hebrew names the Meunites or Maon, a people from the area south of the Dead Sea (2 Chronicles 26:7). Judges never tells of an oppression by them. Both Greek texts read "Midian," which would complete the list with Gideon's enemy, and many translators follow it. Others keep "Maon" as the harder reading, perhaps a group allied with the Midianites or Amalekites. See the variant.

a: That is why I will rescue you no more.
p: For once God says no to Israel's cry. Then, after real repentance, he relents. Readers explain this in different ways.
b: Earlier in the book Israel's cry is answered at once (3:9, 15; 4:3; 6:7). Here God refuses and mocks: "Go and cry to the gods you have picked" (10:14). Some see this as a test of the depth of Israel's repentance, which then comes with deeds: they put away the foreign gods (10:16). Others see God's patience truly at an end, and the rescue that follows through Jephthah as a mixed blessing: Jephthah is chosen by the elders, not by God. The scene echoes Moses' warnings (Deuteronomy 32:37–38) and Jeremiah 2:28.

a: So they put away the foreign gods from among them
p: The same act that Jacob's family and Joshua's Israel performed at Shechem.
b: Jacob told his household, "Put away the foreign gods in your midst" (Genesis 35:2), and Joshua repeated the call at Shechem (Joshua 24:23). Samuel will say it again at Mizpah (1 Samuel 7:3–4). This is the only time in Judges that the Israelites do more than cry out: they act. Whether it is lasting repentance or a bargaining move the text leaves open.

a: And the LORD had had enough of Israel's misery.
p: The verb means to grow short or impatient. Did God pity Israel, or grow tired of their pleading? Both readings exist.
b: Vattiqtsar nafsho, literally "his soul became short," is used for growing impatient or worn out (Numbers 21:4; 16:16, of Samson worn down by Delilah). 'Amal can mean Israel's "misery" or their "troublemaking." Most readers take it as compassion: God could no longer stand to see them suffer. Some, like Webb and Block, read it as weariness with Israel's endless cycle: God has had enough of their fickle behavior, and gives them a judge without much hope. The Plain English keeps both open.
orig: וַתִּקְצַר נַפְשׁוֹ בַּעֲמַל יִשְׂרָאֵל (vattiqtsar nafsho ba'amal Yisra'el)

a: pitched camp at Mizpah
p: "Watchtower" in Gilead, where Jacob and Laban made their treaty. Jephthah's home and gathering place.
b: Mitspah means "lookout" or "watchtower," and several places had the name. This one is east of the Jordan in Gilead, probably where Jacob and Laban set up a heap of stones and said, "May the LORD keep watch between me and you" (Genesis 31:49). Jephthah will make his agreement with the elders "before the LORD at Mizpah" (11:11) and his house is there (11:34). Its exact site is uncertain. A different Mizpah in Benjamin hosts the assembly of chapters 20–21.

a: he was the son of a prostitute
p: Jephthah's mother was a prostitute. As her son he had no right to inherit, so his half-brothers drove him out.
b: A zonah was a woman who sold sex, though some scholars think the word may also cover a foreign or unregistered wife. A prostitute's son had no clear place in his father's clan. The half-brothers' words echo Sarah's demand to drive out Hagar's son (Genesis 21:10). "Gilead" is both the region and the name of Jephthah's father here; some think it means only that his father was an unknown Gileadite. Jephthah joins a line of rejected men God uses, but his upbringing among outlaws shapes the bargainer he becomes.

a: the land of Tob
p: A district north-east of Gilead, toward Aram. Later it sent soldiers to fight David.
b: Tob means "good." The area lay east of the Sea of Galilee, near the edge of Aram. In David's time the Ammonites hired twelve thousand men from Tob against Israel (2 Samuel 10:6–8). Egyptian lists and the Amarna letters may also name it. It was frontier country, out of reach of town elders, where an outlaw band could live by raiding.

a: Come and lead us as commander
p: The elders offer qatsin, a field commander. Jephthah holds out for rosh, "head" for life, and wins it.
b: Qatsin means an officer or chief, here a war leader for the campaign (Joshua 10:24). Jephthah answers with a grievance, and the elders raise their offer: "you will be our head, over all the people of Gilead" (11:8). Head is rosh, a lasting title. He then makes sure the title holds after victory (11:9). The scene reads like a market bargain, and it shows Jephthah's skill with words, the same skill he will use with Ammon and, fatally, with God. In 11:11 he receives both titles.

a: The LORD will be the one who hears between us.
p: An oath formula: God hears the agreement and will punish whoever breaks it.
b: Agreements in the ancient world were sworn before gods as witnesses, who would punish the side that broke faith. Laban and Jacob say at Mizpah, "May the LORD keep watch between me and you" (Genesis 31:49), and Jeremiah's hearers say, "May the LORD be a true and faithful witness against us" (Jeremiah 42:5). Jephthah then repeats the terms "before the LORD at Mizpah" (11:11), making it a sworn covenant. His words are binding; so, he will find, are his vows.
orig: יְהוָה יִהְיֶה שֹׁמֵעַ בֵּינוֹתֵינוּ (YHWH yihyeh shomea' benotenu)

a: Because Israel took my land when they came up from Egypt, from the Arnon to the Jabbok
p: Ammon claims the land between two rivers. Jephthah answers with a history lesson drawn from Numbers.
b: The disputed land lay east of the Jordan between the Arnon (Wadi Mujib) in the south and the Jabbok (Wadi Zarqa) in the north. According to Numbers, Israel took it from Sihon king of the Amorites, who had himself taken it from Moab (Numbers 21:21–31). Ammon's real territory was further east, around Rabbah (modern Amman). Jephthah's letter (11:15–27) follows the route of Numbers 20–21 and Deuteronomy 2 closely: Edom and Moab refused passage, Israel went around, and Sihon attacked. It is one of the longest diplomatic speeches in the Bible.
r: Numbers 20:14–21; Numbers 21:13; Numbers 21:21–31; Deuteronomy 2:9; Deuteronomy 2:19; Deuteronomy 2:24–36

a: Whatever your god Chemosh gives you to possess
p: Chemosh was Moab's god, not Ammon's. Jephthah seems to speak as if other nations' gods are real. Readers explain both.
b: Chemosh was Moab's national god (Numbers 21:29; the Mesha Stele), while Ammon's was Milcom (1 Kings 11:5). Some scholars think the speech was first addressed to Moab, or that Ammon now ruled Moabite land, or that Jephthah lumped the two together. The Mesha Stele (about 840 BC) speaks exactly this way: Chemosh was angry with his land and later gave it back to Moab. As for the theology, many readers see Jephthah arguing on the king's own terms, not admitting that Chemosh exists. Others see a stage of belief in which each nation had its god, and the LORD was Israel's.
r: Numbers 21:29; 1 Kings 11:5–7; 1 Kings 11:33; 2 Kings 3:27; Deuteronomy 32:8–9; Micah 4:5

a: Did he ever pick a quarrel with Israel?
p: Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel but did not go to war. Joshua 24:9 says he "fought," perhaps meaning by curses.
b: Numbers 22–24 tells how Balak king of Moab hired Balaam to curse Israel, and failed. Jephthah's point is that Balak never went to war over the land. Joshua 24:9 says that Balak "got up and fought against Israel," perhaps meaning the war of curses, or the seduction at Peor (Numbers 25). Micah 6:5 remembers Balak's scheme too. Jephthah's history is selective, as diplomatic letters are, but it is accurate to the main story in Numbers.

a: For three hundred years
p: Jephthah's "300 years" is used in debates about the date of the exodus. It may be a round number.
b: If taken literally, three hundred years from the conquest of Sihon to Jephthah fits an exodus in the fifteenth century BC (see 1 Kings 6:1's 480 years). Those who date the exodus to the thirteenth century note that adding the book's numbers makes a figure too large for any date, so the periods must overlap or be rounded. Jephthah may also be rounding up for effect in a diplomatic letter; adding the years from 3:8 to 10:8 gives about 300. Either way, his point is that Israel's claim was old and unchallenged.

a: Let the LORD, the Judge, be judge today
p: The only place in the book where the title "the Judge" is given, and it is given to God.
b: The book is called Judges, yet no human leader is ever called "the judge" (hashofet) as a title. Jephthah gives the title to the LORD. Abraham asked, "Will the Judge of all the earth not do what is just?" (Genesis 18:25). Many readers see this as a key to the book: the real Judge of Israel is God, and the human judges only carry out his rescue. Gideon refused rule for the same reason (8:23).

a: Jephthah now had the Spirit of the LORD on him.
p: The Spirit comes on Jephthah before he vows. Why did he need to bargain? Readers see it as faith or as doubt.
b: With Othniel (3:10) and Gideon (6:34), the Spirit's coming led to victory. Here the Spirit comes on Jephthah, and then he still makes a vow to secure the win (11:30). Many readers, Jewish and Christian, see the vow as needless, an act of unbelief or of the bargaining habit of his whole life: he dealt with his brothers, the elders and Ammon in the same way. Others see it as the normal piety of a soldier before battle, like Israel's vow at Hormah (Numbers 21:2). The Spirit's gift did not make Jephthah wise.

a: whatever comes out, whatever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me
p: Did Jephthah expect an animal or a person? The Hebrew can mean either. Houses then kept animals inside.
b: The Hebrew hayyotse is "the one coming out" or "whatever comes out"; it does not say whether a person or animal. Four-room houses of the period often kept livestock on the ground floor, so an animal could come out of the door. But "to meet me" (liqra'ti) is something people do, and victory was greeted by women with song (Exodus 15:20; 1 Samuel 18:6). Many readers think Jephthah expected a human, perhaps a servant, and so made a terrible vow. Others think he expected an animal and was caught out.
orig: הַיּוֹצֵא אֲשֶׁר יֵצֵא מִדַּלְתֵי בֵיתִי (hayyotse asher yetse middalte veti)

a: and I will offer it up as a burnt offering
p: Some Jewish and Christian commentators read the "and" as "or": it will be the LORD's, or a burnt offering if fit.
b: The Hebrew joins the two parts with ve-, usually "and." Rabbi David Kimchi (Radak), citing his father Joseph, read it as "or": if a person came out, they would be dedicated to God; if a clean animal, it would be offered. Abraham ibn Ezra, on the vow laws of Leviticus 27, also mentions the reading. Its defenders note that "will be the LORD's" is the language of dedication, as when Hannah gives Samuel to the LORD "all the days of his life" (1 Samuel 1:11, 28). Most modern scholars think the plain sense is "and," one vow with two parts, and that the story records a real sacrifice. See the note at 11:39 for the whole debate.

a: His daughter was coming out to meet him, with tambourines and dancing.
p: Women met victors with music and dance, as Miriam did after the sea. Jephthah's daughter does what women did.
b: After the crossing of the sea, "Miriam the prophet, Aaron's sister, took a tambourine in her hand" and the women went out with tambourines and dancing (Exodus 15:20). Women greeted Saul and David the same way (1 Samuel 18:6). The words "to meet him" repeat the vow (11:31). The daughter does exactly what custom expected, and that is what makes the scene unbearable.

a: She was his one and only child.
p: The words recall Abraham and Isaac, "your son, your only one." But no voice from heaven stops Jephthah.
b: Yechidah, "only one," is the word God uses of Isaac: "Take your son, please, your only one, whom you love" (Genesis 22:2). Many readers, ancient and modern, set the two stories side by side. In Genesis God commands the offering and then stops it; here God commands nothing and says nothing. Pseudo-Philo has God angry at the vow, saying, "what if a dog had met him?" The silence of God in Judges 11 is part of the story's horror. The narrator adds, "Apart from her he had neither son nor daughter": Jephthah's line ends with her.

a: You are the one bringing me ruin!
p: The word 'akhar, "bring trouble," was used of Achan, whose sin brought disaster on Israel.
b: 'Okhar is to bring disaster on someone. Achan, whose theft brought defeat at Ai, was stoned in the Valley of Achor, "Trouble" (Joshua 7:25–26). Elijah is called "the troubler of Israel" by Ahab, who answers that Ahab is the troubler (1 Kings 18:17–18). Jephthah blames his daughter for his own vow. Many readers note his first thought is for himself: "you have brought me low." He also says "I opened my mouth to the LORD," a phrase his daughter takes up with more dignity (11:36).

a: I opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot go back on it.
p: The law said vows must be kept. But it also allowed redeeming a person with money, and forbade human sacrifice.
b: "When a man makes a vow to the LORD ... he must not break his word" (Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:21–23). Yet the law gave prices for redeeming people vowed to God (Leviticus 27:1–8), and it called child sacrifice detestable (Deuteronomy 12:31; 18:10). The rabbis argued that Jephthah could have had his vow annulled or paid money, and blamed both him and the priest Phinehas, who would not go to him out of pride (Genesis Rabbah 60:3; Leviticus Rabbah 37:4). Ecclesiastes 5:4–6 warns against rash vows.

a: go down into the hills
p: The Hebrew says "go down on the hills." Some scholars change one letter to read "wander."
b: The Hebrew veyaradti 'al-heharim is "and I will go down on the mountains." One goes up into hills, not down, so some scholars change the verb to vearadti, from rud, "to roam" (compare Jeremiah 2:31), and many translations have "roam" or "wander." Others keep the Hebrew: from a town such as Mizpah one could go down to the hill slopes or the wild country beyond, and "go down" may simply mean leaving home. The Plain English follows the Hebrew as written.

a: weep over my virginity
p: Bethulim means the state of being a young woman of marrying age. She mourns a life without marriage and children.
b: Betulim can mean virginity or the time of youth before marriage. The daughter does not mourn her death as such, but that she will die young, unmarried and childless, with no one to carry on her or her father's name. In Israel, to die childless was a great sorrow. Her request for two months among "the hills" with her friends gives her a voice and a ritual of grief. Those who think she was dedicated rather than killed point to this phrase and to 11:39, "She had never slept with a man."

a: he did to her the vow he had made
p: The text never says she died. Most ancient readers believed she was sacrificed. The next note gives the case for dedication.
b: The narrator turns away at the key moment. The case for a sacrifice starts from the words: Jephthah vowed a burnt offering, and "he did to her the vow he had made." Pseudo-Philo names her Seila and has her lament before she dies. Josephus says Jephthah sacrificed her, "a sacrifice neither lawful nor pleasing to God." The Targum adds that Phinehas could have released him. The rabbis treated it as a real sacrifice and a sin, and Augustine judged it a sacrifice too. The narrator echoes Isaac, the "one and only" child Abraham was told to offer (11:34; Genesis 22:2), and that story too turns on a burnt offering. Against the dedication view, the Bible knows no custom of women living unmarried for life at a sanctuary, and "she had never slept with a man" can simply mean she died childless. Modern readers such as Phyllis Trible read the silence as part of the horror.

a: She had never slept with a man.
p: Some Jewish and Christian scholars argue that she lived on, unmarried, in God's service.
b: From the Middle Ages Kimchi, and Christian scholars such as Keil and Delitzsch, Hengstenberg and many later evangelicals, argued that Jephthah's daughter was dedicated rather than killed. They point to the "or" reading of 11:31 and the dedication sense of "will be the LORD's," as with Samuel (1 Samuel 1:11, 28); to her mourning for her virginity, not her life, and this line, which would be pointless after a death; to women who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting (Exodus 38:8; 1 Samuel 2:22); to the law that let a vowed person be redeemed (Leviticus 27:1–8) and the ban on human sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31); to the yearly visits of 11:40, read as "to talk with her"; and to Hebrews 11:32, which lists Jephthah among the faithful.
r: 11:31; 11:37; 11:40; 1 Samuel 1:11; 1 Samuel 1:28; Exodus 38:8; 1 Samuel 2:22; Leviticus 27:1–8; Deuteronomy 12:31; Hebrews 11:32

a: to retell the story of the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite
p: The verb tannot means to retell, as in 5:11. Kimchi read it as "to talk with her": the women visited her each year.
b: Letannot is from tanah, the verb used in the Song of Deborah for retelling the LORD's righteous acts at the wells (5:11). The women "retell" or "commemorate" her, keeping her memory alive since she had no children to do so. Older translations have "lament." Kimchi took the phrase letannot lebat-Yiftach as "to talk with Jephthah's daughter," that is, to console her, which assumes she was alive and living apart; this is one of the main supports of the dedication view (see the note at 11:39). No such custom is mentioned anywhere else, and some scholars think the story explains an old women's festival. The daughter's name is never given, but her story is the one told.

a: We will burn your house down over you!
p: Ephraim complained to Gideon and was calmed with soft words. Jephthah answers with war.
b: After Gideon's victory, Ephraim protested that it had not been called (8:1), and Gideon soothed them: "What have I done that compares with you?" (8:2–3). Now Ephraim makes the same complaint, with a threat to burn Jephthah's house. The Philistines will make the same threat to Samson's bride (14:15). Jephthah, who has just lost his daughter, does not answer softly. The book's tribes are drifting from quarrels toward civil war, which comes in full in chapters 20–21.

a: I put my life in my palm
p: An idiom for risking one's life. David and Samuel's audience used it too.
b: "I put my life (nefesh) in my palm": to hold one's life in an open hand, where it could easily be lost. David is said to have done this in fighting Goliath (1 Samuel 19:5), and the woman of Endor in obeying Saul (1 Samuel 28:21). Psalm 119:109 says, "My life is in my palm all the time." Jephthah says he risked everything alone because Ephraim did not answer his call. There is no record of that call in chapter 11.

a: You are runaways from Ephraim
p: Ephraim's insult: the Gileadites are fugitives, not a true tribe. In 12:5 the same word turns on Ephraim.
b: Pelite Efrayim, "escapees of Ephraim," sneers that the people east of the Jordan are deserters who ran off and settled among other tribes. The Hebrew is hard and some think part of it was copied twice. The irony is sharp: in the next verse the defeated Ephraimites become the "runaways" (pelite Efrayim, 12:5) trying to cross the river. The insult is thrown back on those who spoke it.

a: Say 'Shibboleth.'
p: A test word: the Ephraimites said "s" where the Gileadites said "sh." A real dialect difference, long debated.
b: Shibbolet means "ear of grain" or "flowing stream," a fitting word to ask at a river crossing. The Ephraimites said sibbolet. Scholars have proposed several sound differences that might lie behind the spelling, since Hebrew letters for "s" and "sh" were close; E. A. Speiser and others linked it to a known dialect feature. The point is clear: dialect betrayed a man's tribe. "Shibboleth" entered English as a word for any test phrase or custom that marks insiders from outsiders.

a: Forty-two thousand of Ephraim fell
p: A huge toll for a civil clash. Some read 'elef as "units" rather than "thousand."
b: Forty-two thousand is a larger toll than many foreign wars in the book. Readers who take the number at face value see the scale of the disaster: Israel killed more of its own than Jephthah killed Ammonites. Others, following George Mendenhall, think 'elef in old military lists meant a clan unit, so the figure would be 42 units, far fewer men. Either way the point stands: the judge's sword now falls on Israel itself, a step toward the civil war of chapter 20.

a: in one of the towns of Gilead
p: The Hebrew says "in the towns of Gilead," plural. The Greek reads "in his town." A midrash made a grim tale of it.
b: The Hebrew reads be'are Gil'ad, "in the towns of Gilead." Most translations say "one of the towns," and the Greek reads "in his town, Gilead" or "in his town in Gilead" (see the variant). A rabbinic midrash took the plural literally: as punishment for his vow, Jephthah's limbs fell off one by one, and each was buried where it fell (Genesis Rabbah 60:3). Jephthah judged only six years, the shortest term in the book.

a: Ibzan of Bethlehem
p: The Talmud identifies Ibzan with Boaz of Bethlehem. Most scholars think this Bethlehem was in Zebulun.
b: The Babylonian Talmud says, "Ibzan is Boaz" (Bava Batra 91a), linking this judge of Bethlehem with Ruth's husband, and it adds that his sixty children all died in his lifetime. Most modern scholars think this is a different Bethlehem, in Zebulun (Joshua 19:15), since the judges around him come from the north. The book of Ruth is set "In the days when the judges ruled" (Ruth 1:1), and Bethlehem in Judah links Judges 17–21 to Ruth and David.

a: The daughters he sent outside
p: Ibzan married his children outside his clan, building alliances. Sixty marriages is a sign of wealth and reach.
b: Hachutsah, "outside," means outside his clan or tribe. Arranging marriages across clans tied families together and spread a leader's influence, much as kings did later with foreign marriages. Thirty sons and thirty daughters shows a large household, probably with several wives (compare 8:30). The writer may be noting quietly that Ibzan's power rested on family politics rather than on rescuing Israel.

a: They buried him at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.
p: Elon and Aijalon are spelled with the same consonants in Hebrew. The man and his burial place share a name.
b: In Hebrew Elon is 'Elon and the place is 'Ayyalon, both written with the same letters ('ylwn, אילון). The Greek reads "Ailon" for both. The burial place may have been named after him, or he after it, or the story may preserve a clan's link to a place. This Aijalon in Zebulun is not the better-known Aijalon in the Shephelah (1:35; Joshua 10:12).

a: in the hill country of the Amalekites
p: An odd note: Amalekites in Ephraim. The Song of Deborah also links Ephraim with Amalek (5:14).
b: Amalek was a desert people of the south (Exodus 17:8–16; 1 Samuel 15:7). Yet this note places "the hill country of the Amalekites" in Ephraim, and the Song of Deborah says Ephraim's "root is in Amalek" (5:14). The name may preserve a memory of an Amalekite group who once lived in the central hills, or it may be an old place name. Pirathon is probably modern Far'ata, west of Shechem. Benaiah, one of David's mighty men, came from there (2 Samuel 23:30).
